articles.title: Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson is appealing - here's what you need to know
articles.summary: The Australian, who notoriously poisoned her family members, is trying to overturn her conviction.
articles.body:
A year after her blockbuster trial, Australia's notorious mushroom murderer is facing court again, in a bid to overturn her conviction.

Erin Patterson was jailed for life last September for murdering three relatives and trying to kill another with a toxic mushroom meal she served at her home in Leongatha, Victoria, in 2023.

But the 51-year-old says she did not receive a fair trial, citing problems with evidence, the actions of the prosecution, and an unusual mishap with the jury while they deliberated on their verdicts.

At the same time that Erin Patterson's case is heard, prosecutors will also be appealing her sentence. The judge said Patterson could apply for parole after 33 years, but the prosecution says that's "manifestly inadequate" and the triple murderer should never be freed.

Patterson killed her in-laws Don and Gail Patterson, both 70, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, 66, after serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms at her home in rural Victoria in 2023.

Heather's husband, Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, survived the lunch after weeks in hospital and still has ongoing health issues related to the poisoning.

Patterson's estranged husband, Simon Patterson, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.

After the trial, it was revealed that he had become so violently ill after eating several of her meals in the past that he had been in a coma, a large part of his bowel had been surgically removed, and his family were told to say goodbye to him twice as he was not expected to survive his ailments.

Erin Patterson maintained throughout the trial that she never meant to kill her relatives - that it was all a terrible accident, and her lies and attempts to dispose of evidence in the aftermath of the lunch were because she was panicking she would be blamed for the deaths.

Patterson won't be attending the appeal in person. She's chosen to appear via video link from Dame Phyllis Frost Centre, the maximum security prison on the outskirts of Melbourne where she's serving her sentence.

Last November, her legal team filed a three-page document outlining the arguments they plan to make in an effort to overturn her conviction.

There are seven grounds for this appeal, which will be heard by three judges.

Firstly, there are bits of evidence Patterson's lawyers say the jurors should never have seen: for example, mobile phone tracking data that indicated she'd travelled to places where death cap mushrooms were recently spotted.

Her lawyers also argue that evidence from "Facebook friends" should not have been allowed. That included online messages in which she ranted about her in-laws as well as her estranged husband Simon Patterson, at one point calling him a "deadbeat".

All that evidence, Patterson's team says, was not relevant and prejudicial, causing a substantial miscarriage of justice.

But her lawyers also argue that other pieces of evidence would have helped Patterson in court. Photos and images relating to her hobby as a long-time mushroom forager - and supporting their argument that the deaths were a tragic accident - had been wrongly excluded, the defence says.

Then there are their issues with the prosecution. Patterson's team say they were inconsistent about a motive, starting the trial by saying they wouldn't argue a particular motive, but ending it by implying there was one.

They also criticise the five days Patterson was cross-examined by barrister Nannette Rogers. At times it felt tense witnessing the two sparring in the courtroom, with Rogers accusing her of repeatedly lying. Patterson argues it was "unfair and oppressive".

But the most intriguing aspect of the appeal document submitted by Erin Patterson's lawyers relates to the jury deliberations.

Because there was so much hype around the case, there were steps taken throughout the trial to ensure the jury wasn't influenced by friends, family or the media. When they began deliberating, they had to stay in supervised accommodation, with little to no contact with the outside world, until they reached a decision.

But according to Patterson's lawyers, a "fundamental irregularity" occurred which "fatally undermined" the integrity of the verdicts.

It turns out that room shortages caused by the media frenzy in the regional towns around the courthouse meant the jury wound up sharing a hotel with members of the prosecution, a key police witness, and journalists.

The jury had a whole hotel floor to themselves, and the judge at the time said there was no evidence they had any interaction with anyone linked to the case.

Patterson's team didn't raise any concerns during the trial, but in their appeal filing said: "[This] requires the quashing of the convictions and an order for a re-trial so that justice cannot only be done but be seen to be done."

The Department of Public Prosecutions (DPP) is appealing over the length of Patterson's sentence.

Justice Christopher Beale last year agreed that Patterson's crimes were the worst of their kind, but said his decision to allow parole after 33 years was influenced by the "harsh prison conditions" she faced.

He noted that she'd already spent 15 months in solitary confinement at the time of her sentencing. In solitary confinement, prisoners cannot mix and meals are delivered via a small opening in the cell door.

For her own safety, he added, there was a "substantial chance" that she would be held in an isolation wing "for years to come" because of the notoriety of her case.

The outcome of the appeal will not be known immediately after these hearings as the decision could take months.

If the three judges in the Court of Appeal choose to overturn her convictions, there are two options: a retrial or acquittal.

If the prosecution's appeal is successful, Erin Patterson could see her parole period being extended beyond 33 years. Or she may even be sentenced to life without parole.

articles.title: 'Welcome home, bab,' Call the Midwife star back in Brum
articles.summary: Helen George said the Alexandra Theatre was one of the first she visited as a child.
articles.body:
Birmingham-born actress Helen George has said it is "so lovely" to be performing again in her home city, in a stage revival of the classic 1956 film musical High Society.

George, who plays Trixie Aylward in the hit BBC drama Call the Midwife, is at the Alexandra Theatre this week at the start of a UK tour, alongside film and TV star Freddie Fox.

She said audiences in Birmingham are "so kind, responsive and lovely", and added that theatre bosses had left "a big bar of Cadbury chocolate saying 'welcome home, bab'" in her dressing room.

The former Strictly Come Dancing contestant, who grew up in the Harborne area of the city, promised to take her co-star Fox for a Balti during their run.

The 1956 film version of High Society starred Frank Sinatra, Bing Crosby and Grace Kelly, with music and lyrics by Cole Porter.

Freddie Fox plays the Sinatra character, cynical tabloid journalist Mike Connor, in his first musical theatre role, which started life earlier this year with a run at London's Barbican.

The star of films including Pride and television shows including House of the Dragon and Slow Horses said the role fulfils a "childhood ambition", and that "to be able to sing a songbook like this, by one of the best lyricists and composers who's ever lived, is a complete dream come true for me".

Fox is the brother of actor Emilia Fox, star of BBC drama Silent Witness, which moved production to Birmingham in 2024.

He said his sister "loves it" in the city, and "always speaks very fondly of Birmingham", adding that he too loved performing at the Birmingham Repertory theatre a few years ago.

George said her Call the Midwife character, who spends most of her time in gritty east end London, had several unlikely parallels with the 1930s New York socialite she plays in High Society.

"They both like their alcohol, they're both quite fun characters, and they both like the boys. I'm not typecast at all, obviously," she said.

Asked whether she would be returning to her breakout role in Call the Midwife, which drew nine million viewers at its peak, Helen George said she was "waiting to find out" if the show would return for a new series next year, "and potentially a film, which would be wonderful".

High Society is on at the Alexandra Theatre in Birmingham until Saturday 22 August, as part of a UK tour until November.

articles.title: Former Fauci adviser David Morens pleads guilty to conspiring to conceal Covid-19 records
articles.summary: David Morens, who worked under Fauci ‌as a senior official at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases during the pandemic, faces up to five years in prison.
articles.body: A former adviser to infectious disease expert Anthony Fauci pleaded guilty Tuesday to conspiring to evade public records laws and conceal government documents related to ​grant research funding and the Covid-19 pandemic. David Morens, who had worked under Fauci ‌as a senior official at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases during the pandemic, entered his plea to a conspiracy charge during a hearing in federal court in Greenbelt, Maryland. The 78-year-old had been indicted ​in April on charges related to what prosecutors said was a scheme to thwart ​public records requests received by the agency beginning in April 2020 related ⁠to Covid-19 research grants. He faces up to five years in prison when he is sentenced ​on Nov. 12. “By pleading guilty today, Dr. Morens has taken responsibility for what he did, ​and he will continue to do so,” Timothy Belevetz, his lawyer, said in a statement. The plea came after Fauci, who led the NIAID for 38 years and became the face of the U.S. pandemic response, ​appeared before a Senate panel last month and repeatedly invoked his right against self-incrimination as he ​accused Republican Sen. Rand Paul, a longtime adversary from Kentucky, of pursuing an “unhinged” campaign to see him ‌imprisoned. Covid’s ⁠origins remain unresolved. The FBI said in 2023 that a leak from a Wuhan laboratory likely caused the pandemic, a claim China said had “no credibility whatsoever.” The CIA said in January 2025 a lab leak was likely, but with “low confidence,” while four other U.S. intelligence agencies ​and the National Intelligence ​Council believe the virus ⁠most likely emerged via natural transmission from some animal. Prosecutors said that Morens’ plea related to the National Institutes of Health’s decision to ​cancel a research grant related to bat coronavirus, based on allegations that ​Covid-19 emerged ⁠from the Wuhan lab. The China-based lab had received a sub-award from the company that had received the grant. Prosecutors said that Morens pledged to help restore the bat coronavirus grant and counter ⁠the ​narrative Covid-19 leaked from a lab. Anticipating their communications would ​be sought through Freedom of Information Act requests, Morens and others agreed to correspond using Morens’ personal email account ​instead of his government one, prosecutors said.

articles.title: Former kindergarten teacher, 93, found dead as Hawaii residents clean up after storm
articles.summary: Hurricane Lala tore roofs off houses, uprooted trees and left many households without electricity for days.
articles.body: HONOLULU — A beloved former kindergarten teacher who taught generations of residents in a small town on Hawaii’s Big Island was one of two people whose deaths authorities blamed on a hurricane that lashed the state over the weekend with heavy rain and strong winds. May Doi, 93, was found dead Monday after she was reported missing, police said. Neighbors think she was escaping floodwaters in her home and trying to get to a nearby shelter, said ʻĀina Akamu, a former student of Doi’s who is now a vice principal at a local school. She taught for so long at Naalehu Elementary on the island’s southern tip that “Mrs. Doi was my dad’s kindergarten teacher,” Akamu said Wednesday. “She taught grandkids of her students,” he said. “She was a fixture in this community.” Akamu often saw her taking walks around the small, rural, sugar plantation-era town: “She was so strong.” He recalled how everyone looked forward to having Mrs. Doi as a teacher because she sometimes allowed students to have sleepovers in her classroom. Her deceased husband was a math teacher, Akamu said. The body of a man in his 60s was located by residents in a pasture on Tuesday, a day after police were asked to conduct a welfare check, police said. Authorities said it was the second death attributed to the storm and have not yet released his identity. Residents were struggling to clean up after Hurricane Lala tore roofs off houses, uprooted trees, covered roads in mud and rock and left many households without electricity for days. On top of all that, forecasters warned of the likelihood of another tropical cyclone forming southeast of the islands. ‘We just ask the ancestors to protect us’ Akamu also lamented the destruction of two cemeteries, including one where Akamu’s ancestors have been buried since 1850. Caskets were sticking out of the ground through the town, home to about 800 people, and headstones littered the roadway, he said. “Our graveyard is now scattered all over the community and how do we heal from that?” he said. He worries crews working to clear roads could inadvertently run over remains. “Don’t clear the road, my grandma could be in there,” he said. “That’s what makes me most emotional, it’s like you lost them again.” Akamu was trying to focus on helping his community recover by setting up a hub where residents can get donated items. They are in most need of generators, gasoline and propane, he said. “We just ask the ancestors to protect us,” Akamu said of the threat of another storm. Now well west of Hawaii’s main islands, Lala has reached major Category 3 strength with top sustained winds of 115 mph on Wednesday in what the National Hurricane Center called the first major hurricane of 2026 in the Central Pacific Ocean. But Hawaii residents were put on notice for another storm system, located far to the east-southeast. The hurricane center said conditions appeared conducive for a tropical depression to form within days. It’s too early to tell the exact location or potential wind, rain and storm surge impacts. However, “interests in the Hawaiian Islands should closely monitor the progress of this system,” the hurricane center said, adding it could be a hurricane when it moves near or over the islands by the weekend. Power repairs could take weeks Work continued to clear away tons of mud and debris left behind by a torrent of water that inundated buildings, some of whose roofs were sheared off by the winds. Dozens of homes were washed from foundations, bridges were damaged and a collapsed section of a two-lane road had cut off access to the community of Pahala. The U.S. Department of Transportation approved an initial $6 million in emergency relief to help repair transportation infrastructure damaged by Lala, U.S. Sen. Brian Schatz of Hawaii said. The heaviest recorded rainfall, 43.54 inches, occurred in Laupahoehoe on the northeast coast of the Big Island, the National Weather Service said. About 17,000 customers on the Big Island remained without power on Wednesday, the Hawaiian Electric utility said. Some customers on the islands of Oahu and Maui were still in the dark. Repairs in the heavily damaged areas of the Big Island, including the southern end, could take at least two weeks, the utility said. Lala was moving to the northwest at 10 mph and was expected to turn toward the north early Thursday. It was bearing down on a remote area at the northwestern edge of the Hawaiian Archipelago. Hurricane warnings were posted for portions of the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument from Lisianski Island to Maro Reef. The weather service said the storm was forecast to veer east of the Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge. The population in one of the most remote places on Earth consists entirely of a few dozen U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service staff, volunteers and contractors. Forecasters said there were no tropical-related advisories for the Midway Atoll and any impact might include some elevated surf with a limited amount of rain.

However, “interests in the Hawaiian Islands should closely monitor the progress of this system,” the hurricane center said, adding it could be a hurricane when it moves near or over the islands by the weekend. Power repairs could take weeks Work continued to clear away tons of mud and debris left behind by a torrent of water that inundated buildings, some of whose roofs were sheared off by the winds. Dozens of homes were washed from foundations, bridges were damaged and a collapsed section of a two-lane road had cut off access to the community of Pahala. The U.S. Department of Transportation approved an initial $6 million in emergency relief to help repair transportation infrastructure damaged by Lala, U.S. Sen. Brian Schatz of Hawaii said. The heaviest recorded rainfall, 43.54 inches, occurred in Laupahoehoe on the northeast coast of the Big Island, the National Weather Service said. About 17,000 customers on the Big Island remained without power on Wednesday, the Hawaiian Electric utility said. Some customers on the islands of Oahu and Maui were still in the dark. Repairs in the heavily damaged areas of the Big Island, including the southern end, could take at least two weeks, the utility said. Lala was moving to the northwest at 10 mph and was expected to turn toward the north early Thursday. It was bearing down on a remote area at the northwestern edge of the Hawaiian Archipelago. Hurricane warnings were posted for portions of the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument from Lisianski Island to Maro Reef. The weather service said the storm was forecast to veer east of the Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge. The population in one of the most remote places on Earth consists entirely of a few dozen U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service staff, volunteers and contractors. Forecasters said there were no tropical-related advisories for the Midway Atoll and any impact might include some elevated surf with a limited amount of rain.

articles.title: Australian hiker's body recovered as police probe error reporting she was alive
articles.summary: The body of Lily Hooper, 18, has been airlifted from a national park in the Southern Highlands following an eight-day search.
articles.body:
The body of missing Australian hiker Lily Hooper has been recovered as officials investigate a "miscommunication" that briefly reported she had been found alive.

Within minutes of reports first emerging that she was alive on Thursday, police confirmed that Hooper had been found deceased in the bushland of the Southern Highlands in New South Wales (NSW).

State Premier Chris Minns and NSW police commissioner Mal Lanyon apologised to her family on Friday for the error.

Hooper, 18, an experienced hiker, was reported missing last week, triggering an eight-day search that involved approximately 1,000 people.

A police spokesperson confirmed to BBC News on Friday that her body had been airlifted from the Nattai National Park, south-west of Sydney.

"A post-mortem examination will be conducted in coming days to formally confirm ID and determine cause of death," the statement said.

Minns had told a state parliamentary hearing on Thursday that crews had found Hooper alive "with half a bottle of water" eight days after she had been reported missing. Within 30 minutes, he corrected himself saying "Lily's body has been found" and that she was deceased.

Media outlets in Australia widely reported the initial incorrect reports that Hooper was located alive before retracting their stories shortly after.

The miscommunication meant there was a brief window in which her parents believed she was alive.

Minns said on Friday that he planned to speak directly to Hooper's family to issue a personal apology.

"The government, myself – we're profoundly sorry," he said.

NSW State Emergency Services commissioner Mike Wassing said that codes were often assigned during major searches.

Such terms can avoid sensitive details being shared over radio broadcasts during a search, when friends, relatives and community volunteers are usually involved alongside emergency service personnel and police officers.

"The codes are usually associated with some aspect like that in terms of bottles of water," Wassing told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, although he did not confirm the cause of the error under investigation.

Lanyon said communications can be challenging during large searches in remote locations.

"Tragically, her condition was miscommunicated and for that I apologise," he said.

Police will review policy and processes to ensure protocols were "foolproof" into the future, Lanyon added.

articles.title: Torfaen becomes global hotspot for carbon emissions after wildfires
articles.summary: The smell of burning from the Blaenavon wildfire was reported 30 miles away in Cardiff.
articles.body:
A county in Wales had one of the world's highest carbon emissions per square kilometre due to wildfires in July, according to a charity.

The fire above Blaenavon, Torfaen was described as "one of the largest and most challenging" in south Wales in recent years by the fire service.

Save the Children said it was concerned about possible health consequences after data published by the European Union's earth observation programme, Copernicus, showed Torfaen behind Malanje in Angola, Spain's Ávila and Annaba in Algeria in terms of wildfire emissions in July.

Torfaen council said it was unaware of the EU data but its own air quality monitoring showed "elevated particulate concentrations".

A blaze the size of about 300 football pitches broke out on Mynydd Garnclochdy, between Abersychan and Blaenavon, with people reporting smelling smoke about 30 (48km) miles away in Cardiff.

Combined with others across the region it contributed to a major incident being declared , which eventually required assistance from the military .

Blaenavon councillor Janet Jones said the smoke had been "particularly bad" on 13 August - about three weeks after the fire first ignited.

"There was great concern about air quality and the impact on elderly people and those suffering with respiratory issues such as emphysema and COPD."

Jones said she had spoken with GP practice nurses two weeks ago and was not aware of any increase in patients complaining about respiratory problems, but added this "could change in the months ahead".

Melanie Simmonds, head of Save the Children Wales, said: "In Wales and across the world, children are breathing in smoke from wildfires, coping with extreme heat and losing the freedom to play outdoors because the air is no longer safe.

"These conditions are not only frightening - they carry serious health consequences for children whose bodies and lungs are still developing."

Torfaen council said it was not aware of the research and "it is not clear what data or evidence was used in the assessment to arrive at the reported conclusion".

It said it "recognises that prolonged wildfire incidents have the potential to adversely affect local air quality, particularly through increased levels of smoke and particulate matter".

It added it "continuously monitors" air quality through a monitoring station in Croesyceiliog Cwmbran.

"While elevated particulate concentrations have been observed during the wildfire period, the council's monitoring station is intended to provide information on general background air quality rather than conditions at specific locations immediately adjacent to the fires," it said.

The Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) website said it was part of European Union's Space programme, and provided global information related to air pollution and health.

Its data said emissions in Torfaen had been "extremely unusual".

Man tracks down siblings who sent him Christmas present as he fled war 33 years ago

People who want to live on this almost-empty estate aren't allowed to buy the homes

articles.title: Erin Patterson: The hotel booking snafu that could free mushroom murderer
articles.summary: A table tennis tournament and a throat lozenge could help Erin Patterson's lawyers overturn her convictions.
articles.body:
Last July, hundreds descended on Australia's Gippsland region from around the country for the most exciting event on the annual table tennis calendar.

But as elite players vied for medals at the national championships, one of the biggest criminal cases in the nation's history - that of mushroom murderer Erin Patterson - was unfolding just a few kilometres away.

This tournament inadvertently became part of a perfect storm which the triple killer's lawyers are now arguing "fatally undermined" the fairness of her trial.

The jury which condemned Patterson to prison were supposed to be isolated - sheltered from the frenzy surrounding the case while they deliberated.

But accommodation shortages in the region, exacerbated by the table tennis competition, meant they shared a hotel with members of the prosecution, a key police witness, and journalists.

Now Patterson's legal team is trying to overturn her convictions on appeal.

"The only proper remedy is... the order for a re-trial," Patterson's barrister Richard Edney said.

When Patterson served her estranged husband's relatives a poisonous mushroom-laced lunch in 2023, killing three and gravely injuring another, she thrust the sleepy Gippsland region into the global spotlight.

The community of Korumburra, where the victims were beloved figures, became shrouded in grief. Leongatha, where Patterson lived, was gripped by shock. And Morwell, host of the lengthy trial, was overwhelmed by journalists, lawyers and spectators - as were towns nearby.

You couldn't walk down the main street without spotting some of the courtroom's stars, or grab a coffee without overhearing chatter about the case.

Mushroom murders and cancer lie: Nine weeks of evidence that gripped a courtroom

'Everyone knows somebody affected': The small towns in shock after mushroom murders

It was this frenzy from which the jury of 12 needed protection, the trial judge decided.

Jurors are required to consider only the evidence presented to them in court, and must only talk about the case among themselves. In Australia, these rules are so strict that discussion with outsiders is forbidden even after a trial wraps up.

To reduce the risk of contamination and the temptation of gossip, Justice Christopher Beale decided the jury should be sequestered once deliberations began - a relatively rare move which meant they would stay in supervised accommodation with little to no contact with the outside world until they reached a decision.

But finding the jury, and the jury keepers watching them, somewhere to sleep became something of a logistical nightmare.

As the trial dragged on, stays became longer than anyone anticipated and accommodation became a constant scramble.

And the week the table tennis tournament came to town - which by a stroke of bad luck was the one in which the jury finally retired - turned the accommodation drought into a famine.

At 08:28 on Monday 7 July, an email from the judge's chambers popped into the inboxes of the lawyers in the case.

It revealed that the lead detective who investigated the murders - a key trial witness - and two prosecution solicitors had been staying at the same hotel as the sequestered jury.

The jurors had exclusive use of a separate floor of the hotel, the email said, and had eaten their meals in a conference room, away from all other guests.

Common areas like the lobby were used by everyone, but the jury keeper who reported the issue said there had been no interaction between his charges and anyone from the prosecution case.

"I understand that there is a shortage of accommodation in the district, but it is obviously undesirable," Justice Beale wrote.

About two hours later, the prosecution responded, admitting they had been aware of the situation for days.

The detective "took steps to avoid common areas from the point that he became aware that [the jurors] were there", their email read.

Upon learning their team would cross over with the jury for a single night, the prosecution had done its best to find other hotels for staff. But they couldn't get alternative rooms for two solicitors, though the email stressed the pair also took steps to avoid any "incidental contact".

However, another missive from the judge's chambers quickly overshadowed the hotel mix-up that same afternoon: the jury had reached their verdicts.

They had found Patterson guilty on all counts.

Patterson's lawyers are now arguing the hotel mix-up amounted to a "fundamental irregularity" which "fatally undermined" the integrity of the verdicts.

"We would describe... it as catastrophic," Patterson's appeal counsel, Edney, told Victoria's Court of Appeal this week.

"What occurred here was an inexplicable and perhaps still unexplained failure in the process."

The defence - which Edney pointed out had been kept in the dark several days longer than anyone else - didn't immediately move for a mistrial last July.

Instead, it twice asked the state's juries commissioner to investigate in the weeks following the verdicts. Both requests were rejected, the barrister said, and the reasons have not been made public.

A year on, there remains a "vacuum of evidence" around what occurred during "the most critical week" of the entire trial, Edney argued.

There is no CCTV from the hotel; no sworn statements from those who were sharing it with the jury - a group which also includes an unknown number of journalists; and nothing to say what happened except the two brief emails sent last July.

There was also at least one media report at the time - raised by Edney this week but rubbished by the prosecution lawyers as "unverified" and "seemingly inaccurate" - that the mix-up had led to "people hiding in doorways to avoid contact" and "skipping breakfast".

"My question is... so what?" Justice Peter Kidd bit back.

In any criminal trial, jurors see other parties all the time - in corridors, or even nearby cafes - but they're under the constant supervision of jury keepers who have sworn to ensure there's no improper communication, he said.

Edney conceded there was "no evidence" that the jurors had communicated with anyone else, but said innocent contact - even just seeing the detective or solicitors - could have resulted in "subconscious influence".

"This was a hotel with windows," Edney said several times - a likely thing for it to have, someone from the judge's bench countered.

Patterson's team cited two cases to support their argument: one in which jurors were discharged when one was offered a throat lozenge by a defendant's relative during a coughing fit, and another in which a retrial was ordered after jurors caught a taxi without being escorted by a jury keeper.

"The system worked as it was intended to work," Director of Public Prosecutions Brendan Kissane KC said.

The jury was constantly supervised, and when a potential problem was identified, steps were immediately taken to prevent it becoming an actual issue.

The jury keeper, the lead detective, and the prosecution all say there was no contact.

"The evidence in this case is that there was no interaction between any other person and the jury," he said.

Other cases the defence pointed to in which jury errors resulted in retrials all had evidence of actual contact, he noted.

Patterson has seven appeal grounds - the others relating to rulings on evidence and alleged unfairness by the prosecution - but this one, by the defence's own admission, is unprecedented.

Just as important as actual interference is the perception of interference, said Edney, quoting the trial judge's own speech as he selected jury members on the very first day of the trial.

"Justice must not only be done, it must be seen to be done."

The trio of judges are now deliberating on Patterson's appeal, as well as an argument by the prosecution that her parole period should be scrapped.

They will announce their decisions at a later date.

articles.title: Kenya's gold rush: Was it sparked by the discovery of a $200 nugget by a goat herder?
articles.summary: Prospectors have come to West Pokot county in the hope a gram of the precious metal can change their lives.
articles.body:
A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks.

When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; £205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to the arrival of thousands of prospectors in Cheporor.

And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps.

It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.

Even a small amount of the precious metal can transform the futures of these men and women - from Kenya and neighbouring Uganda - many of whose precarious lives rest on an unreliable farming income.

People do sometimes pan for gold in these parts - but rarely find anything significant.

Lomachar's says his discovery came about purely by chance. While he was searching for a missing goat he encountered a group of women panning along a riverbed.

"I joined them, and that's how [the village] realised there was gold in this area," he says.

Farmer and herder Patrick Lokolia, from neighbouring Napawoi village, joined the gold rush hoping to earn some extra money to support his family.

"I have children in school, and paying school fees has been a big problem for me," he tells the BBC wearing an old Chelsea football top and standing amid the mining activity.

Eighteen-year-old Abigael Chelengat says she had never mined before coming to Cheporor from a nearby district, but arrived hoping to find enough gold to pay her school fees and help keep her younger siblings in school.

Behind her hundreds of people work side by side, hacking into the rocky ground with hoes and shovels.

Others carry the earth to a nearby seasonal river, where mostly women crouch in the murky water, washing and sifting mud and sand hoping to detect a tiny trace of the element.

Some of the more experienced miners are deep in holes excavating the earth and drilling at rocks with the same goal.

Hope is kept alive by stories of those for whom the effort has paid off - like Lomachar.

Samuel Kiarie, the deputy commissioner of West Pokot county, says he thinks the rush began after two notable discoveries.

"Young men found what appeared to be a substantial amount of gold. The following day, women made another significant find in the same area," he tells the BBC.

Kiarie explains that women have been finding small quantities of alluvial gold along the same seasonal riverbed for years, typically earning $8-$23 a week.

But the uncovering of larger quantities at the beginning of August is what caught the attention of many people.

Kiarie reckons as rumours spread, the number and size of the discoveries were exaggerated - drawing in ever larger groups of people with little or no mining experience who hoped to replicate the reported early successes.

Since the initial rush, the number of prospectors has gone down to around 2,500 as some have given up the search.

While there is little doubt that some gold has been found in the area, questions remain about the size of the deposit in the earth and its commercial potential.

"I can confirm that small-scale gold traders told us they received an average of about 100 people every day," the deputy commissioner says - though whether the finds were actually gold is not known.

Individual discoveries reportedly range from amounts worth a few hundred Kenyan shillings to one find valued at approximately 78,000 shillings ($600).

West Pokot county borders Uganda, and communities on both sides have long-standing social and family ties.

Mugisha Godfrey, an artisanal miner from Busia in eastern Uganda, travelled to Cheporor after hearing about the discovery from a friend.

He immediately set out for the village spending about 100,000 Ugandan shillings ($27) to get there.

However, the living conditions in Cheporor are not favourable, he says.

"We sleep under the trees, and when morning comes, we continue working. Sometimes we work both day and night," Godfrey tells the BBC.

So far, he has found nothing. But he is not discouraged.

"We can't return unless we find something. Only when we have found what we need can we go back home," he says.

For others, the gold rush has created opportunities without requiring them to dig.

More than 200 businesses have emerged around the site, according to local officials, selling food, water and other essentials to the village's new population.

Irene Ameja travelled from neighbouring Baringo county to cater to the crowds. She sells bottled water, soft drinks, bread, milk and other foodstuffs.

"I am hoping that when I leave, I will have made enough money to continue with my business and expand it," she says.

But the rapid growth of the settlement has also exposed the area's lack of basic services.

"This is a forest and we are in the middle of the mountains," she says. "We don't have clean water to drink or even to bathe."

For women, she adds, the challenges become greater after dark: "You have to find somewhere safe to stay because most of the people sleeping here are men."

Local officials admit the influx has placed enormous pressure on an area with little infrastructure, no piped water and limited sanitation.

Public health officials have been deployed to monitor conditions and help prevent disease outbreaks.

The authorities say they have also increased security patrols amid concerns over sexual violence and the vulnerability of women and girls at the site.

Officials are also worried that children could be drawn into mining activities as schools prepare to reopen in September.

Measures are being put in place to discourage young people from remaining at the site once the new school term begins.

Those still searching are increasingly turning to deeper excavation.

Several truckloads of material have already been transported to nearby Ortum town for processing, with the authorities awaiting the results.

Until then, the size and commercial viability of any mining remain uncertain.

For Lomachar, the answer is not to stop the mining, but to make it more organised.

He wants the government to help local miners establish safer and more effective ways of finding and extracting the gold.

"We would ask the government to help us with things like metal detectors, which could help us find out whether there are other minerals here, so that our community can develop," he says.

He points to the homes nearby as evidence of the area's poverty.

"If you look around, there are hardly any houses with iron-sheet roofs; most are just thatched houses."

paragraphs: A goat herder from a remote area of western Kenya has told the BBC his discovery of a golden nugget has sparked a gold rush, overwhelming his small village over the last few weeks.

When people found out that 33-year-old Manasse Lomachar had sold his three grams of gold for 36,000 Kenyan shillings ($280; £205) several weeks ago, he believes this led to the arrival of thousands of prospectors in Cheporor.
And it is true that what last month was just bushland and rough grazing ground near the village is now scarred by pits, mounds of earth and makeshift mining camps.
It is not clear if was Lomachar's lucky find or other recent discoveries that sparked the excitement. But local authorities estimate that about 10,000 people arrived at the height of the rush.
Even a small amount of the precious metal can transform the futures of these men and women - from Kenya and neighbouring Uganda - many of whose precarious lives rest on an unreliable farming income.
People do sometimes pan for gold in these parts - but rarely find anything significant.
Lomachar's says his discovery came about purely by chance. While he was searching for a missing goat he encountered a group of women panning along a riverbed.
"I joined them, and that's how [the village] realised there was gold in this area," he says.
Farmer and herder Patrick Lokolia, from neighbouring Napawoi village, joined the gold rush hoping to earn some extra money to support his family.
"I have children in school, and paying school fees has been a big problem for me," he tells the BBC wearing an old Chelsea football top and standing amid the mining activity.

Eighteen-year-old Abigael Chelengat says she had never mined before coming to Cheporor from a nearby district, but arrived hoping to find enough gold to pay her school fees and help keep her younger siblings in school.
Behind her hundreds of people work side by side, hacking into the rocky ground with hoes and shovels.
Others carry the earth to a nearby seasonal river, where mostly women crouch in the murky water, washing and sifting mud and sand hoping to detect a tiny trace of the element.
Some of the more experienced miners are deep in holes excavating the earth and drilling at rocks with the same goal.
Hope is kept alive by stories of those for whom the effort has paid off - like Lomachar.
Samuel Kiarie, the deputy commissioner of West Pokot county, says he thinks the rush began after two notable discoveries.
"Young men found what appeared to be a substantial amount of gold. The following day, women made another significant find in the same area," he tells the BBC.
Kiarie explains that women have been finding small quantities of alluvial gold along the same seasonal riverbed for years, typically earning $8-$23 a week.
But the uncovering of larger quantities at the beginning of August is what caught the attention of many people.

Kiarie reckons as rumours spread, the number and size of the discoveries were exaggerated - drawing in ever larger groups of people with little or no mining experience who hoped to replicate the reported early successes.
Since the initial rush, the number of prospectors has gone down to around 2,500 as some have given up the search.
While there is little doubt that some gold has been found in the area, questions remain about the size of the deposit in the earth and its commercial potential.
"I can confirm that small-scale gold traders told us they received an average of about 100 people every day," the deputy commissioner says - though whether the finds were actually gold is not known.
Individual discoveries reportedly range from amounts worth a few hundred Kenyan shillings to one find valued at approximately 78,000 shillings ($600).
West Pokot county borders Uganda, and communities on both sides have long-standing social and family ties.
Mugisha Godfrey, an artisanal miner from Busia in eastern Uganda, travelled to Cheporor after hearing about the discovery from a friend.
He immediately set out for the village spending about 100,000 Ugandan shillings ($27) to get there.
However, the living conditions in Cheporor are not favourable, he says.
"We sleep under the trees, and when morning comes, we continue working. Sometimes we work both day and night," Godfrey tells the BBC.
So far, he has found nothing. But he is not discouraged.
"We can't return unless we find something. Only when we have found what we need can we go back home," he says.
For others, the gold rush has created opportunities without requiring them to dig.
More than 200 businesses have emerged around the site, according to local officials, selling food, water and other essentials to the village's new population.
Irene Ameja travelled from neighbouring Baringo county to cater to the crowds. She sells bottled water, soft drinks, bread, milk and other foodstuffs.
"I am hoping that when I leave, I will have made enough money to continue with my business and expand it," she says.
But the rapid growth of the settlement has also exposed the area's lack of basic services.
"This is a forest and we are in the middle of the mountains," she says. "We don't have clean water to drink or even to bathe."
For women, she adds, the challenges become greater after dark: "You have to find somewhere safe to stay because most of the people sleeping here are men."
Local officials admit the influx has placed enormous pressure on an area with little infrastructure, no piped water and limited sanitation.
Public health officials have been deployed to monitor conditions and help prevent disease outbreaks.
The authorities say they have also increased security patrols amid concerns over sexual violence and the vulnerability of women and girls at the site.
Officials are also worried that children could be drawn into mining activities as schools prepare to reopen in September.
Measures are being put in place to discourage young people from remaining at the site once the new school term begins.
Those still searching are increasingly turning to deeper excavation.
Several truckloads of material have already been transported to nearby Ortum town for processing, with the authorities awaiting the results.
Until then, the size and commercial viability of any mining remain uncertain.
For Lomachar, the answer is not to stop the mining, but to make it more organised.
He wants the government to help local miners establish safer and more effective ways of finding and extracting the gold.
"We would ask the government to help us with things like metal detectors, which could help us find out whether there are other minerals here, so that our community can develop," he says.
He points to the homes nearby as evidence of the area's poverty.
"If you look around, there are hardly any houses with iron-sheet roofs; most are just thatched houses."

articles.title: Sydney Marathon laughs off medal error
articles.summary: Runners will receive a medal at the 2026 Sydney Marathon with an engraving of a German stadium.
articles.body:
The organisers of Sydney Marathon have laughed off a mistake which saw a German stadium etched on to medals for participants, saying "we're not going to run from it".

Questions arose after the event's official social media account unveiled the design of this year's medal earlier in the week, which had mistakenly etched Allianz Arena, based in the German city of Munich, instead of Sydney's Allianz Stadium.

A spokesperson for the Sydney Marathon told the BBC: "A little too much international flavour has found its way onto the back of the finishers medal, with an incorrect depiction of the stadium."

It was "an unfortunate error," they added.

Recognisable Sydney landmarks feature on the double-sided medal, including the Opera House and Harbour Bridge, which are part of the 42.2km (26.2 mile) course.

Users on social media noticed the shape of the stadium engraved on the medal appeared to be carved in the wrong likeness.

Munich's Allianz Arena is sculpted by thousands of diamond-shaped inflatable cushions, while Sydney's similarly named Allianz Stadium has a flatter facade smoothed with long bronze fins.

Sydney Marathon confirmed runners would receive the medal depicting the incorrect city's stadium, noting: "It's a beautiful medal, and now a little more unique."

"It's certainly given everyone something to talk about this weekend, mostly in good humour."

Germany's Allianz Arena also poked fun at the mistake, writing on Instagram: "Oh wow, we didn't have that on our bingo card!"

"Perhaps they tried to find something else they had in common: Allianz Arena -- Sydney Opera -- Unique Architecture -- Both are worth a visit!"

The reverse side of the Sydney Marathon medal shows a gold and indigo pattern designed by First Nations artist Ambrose Killian, widely commended for its ornate pattern.

He confirmed to the BBC that he was not involved in designing the other face of the medal engraved with the wrong stadium.

Some 40,000 runners will take part in the event on 30 August, following more than 120,000 ballot entries.

Organisers praised record participation and fundraising for this year's event.

articles.title: House Speaker Mike Johnson wants the D.C. IndyCar race to be annual: 'I'll be pushing for that'
articles.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson says he wants the Freedom 250 Grand Prix to return every year. The race was routed to avoid needing congressional approval.
articles.body:
House Speaker Mike Johnson said Sunday he wants to bring the Freedom 250 Grand Prix back to Washington every year.

"I want to bring it back next year. I want to make it an annual event," Johnson told Fox News at the race. Asked whether that was possible, he said: "If we have any say in it, we'll be in the majority. I'll be pushing for that."

The race was designed to avoid Congress. Bud Denker, the Penske Corporation president who built the event, took 81 meetings on Capitol Hill between August and January trying to win approval for a course that ran across Capitol grounds. Federal law bars advertising there, and IndyCars are covered in sponsor logos. Denker was not able to get the votes necessary.

So, Denker moved the circuit a block west, outside congressional jurisdiction, and President Trump signed an executive order on Jan. 30 clearing the way without a vote, CNN reported .

Whether it returns is unsettled. Denker has called this year's race "likely a one-off, in this current iteration, at least." Doug Boles, IndyCar's president, said it is "likely just a one-year event." Mayor Muriel Bowser and Trump have both said they want more races in Washington.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, one of two cabinet officials the order directed to designate the route, told Fox News on Sunday the substitute course turned out better than the original.

"I think this is better. The view of the Capitol behind us," Duffy said. "By the way, this is the first time they're going to sell beer on the Mall of the capital, food, festive car race. So I think this venue is probably better than the original thought anyway."

Johnson said 130,000 people were on the Mall on Sunday and that organizers capped attendance for security. Organizers had said they expected about 140,000 each day, against 288,000 ticket requests.

articles.title: 1975 homicide of 27-year-old Norris ‘Snookie’ Evans remains unsolved | Dateline
articles.summary: Norris “Snookie” Evans, a 27-year-old mother of four, was found stabbed to death in her Rochester, New York, home in 1975. Rochester police say the case remains open.
articles.body: In 2021, Tamara Sinclair posted on a local Rochester, New York, Facebook page called “Remember when?” Among its usual posts where members reminisce over long-closed diners and share faded photographs from days gone by, Tamara’s post stood out. She asked if anyone remembered the 1975 murder of her mother, 27-year-old Norris “Snookie” Evans. “My sister was on Facebook and then she just threw that out there,” Daryl Evans told Dateline. A crime author came across Tamara’s post and offered to help her access the Rochester Police Department’s case documents. Tamara says what she read forever altered her understanding of her mother’s death. A life cut short Dateline obtained the same report from the Rochester Police Department. The initial entry states that at 11:24 p.m. on May 23, 1975, Rochester Police dispatch received a phone call reporting “family trouble” at a home on Kron Street in the city’s 19th Ward. According to the report, Officer Paul Camping was dispatched to the scene, where he knocked repeatedly on the front door to no response. Finding the house dark and quiet, he left. The report notes that an hour later, at 12:33 a.m., police received another call: this time from Snookie’s husband, Lewis Evans. Officer Camping returned to the scene and found Lewis “standing outside in an incoherent condition.” He told the responding officer he had just returned home from work at Rochester Products, a local manufacturing company, when he discovered his wife. Snookie was found dead in the living room, “lying face down with her ankles tied together with a white cloth,” according to the police report. The report also notes that a kitchen knife and a cast-iron frying pan were strewn on the floor, and the living room TV was on. Although the home appeared ransacked, there were no signs of forced entry. Lewis told police at the time that $1,100 in cash was missing from a metal box in the living room. The medical examiner’s office determined Snookie had multiple stab wounds and noted she had been nearly decapitated. The estimated time of death was placed between 11:30 p.m. and 12:30 a.m. Tamara was just 3 months old when her mother was killed. Daryl was only 2. Their half brothers on their father’s side were 4 and 6. They were all found inside the home, unharmed. Although Tamara and Daryl have no memories of their mother, the descriptions they’ve heard over the years are consistent: a sweet, devoted parent. Growing up, Snookie was close to her sister, Ellen Evans. “We walked to school together, eat lunch together. We just did everything together,” Ellen told Dateline. “She was the one who kept me grounded. She was the calm.” Gina Alves, married to Snookie and Ellen’s cousin at the time, fondly remembers her friendship with Snookie. “Norris is just so sweet. I really loved her,” Gina told Dateline. “Through her pregnancy, with — what they call him, Tiger — Daryl, he was the cutest baby, and then she got pregnant with her daughter. She was just so excited, you know, ‘Oh, I got a girl! I got a girl!’” Gina says Snookie called her the night she died and asked if she wanted to play cards. “I’ll never forget that I was watching [The] Andy Griffith [Show] and she said, ‘Well, why don’t you guys come over?’” Gina said, choking up. She didn’t end up going. “So then, you know, that happened to her, and I always wonder, maybe if we would’ve went over there, maybe that wouldn’t have happened to her.” Ellen told Dateline she remembers the exact moment their father told her what happened to Snookie. “I slapped him. I slapped him so hard and told him, ‘You’re lying. You’re lying,’” she said. The investigation The Rochester Police Department launched an investigation into Snookie’s killing that would span years, chasing lead after lead. According to their report, Rochester police first looked into those with histories of violent burglaries in the area. They investigated at least 10 people who fit the description, checking fingerprints, administering polygraph exams and checking alibis without making an arrest. Ellen Evans told Dateline the family had its suspicions. She had introduced Snookie to Lewis Evans, the brother of Ellen’s estranged husband. “At first they were happy together,” she said. But as the relationship evolved, Ellen says it became clear to her that Snookie had grown scared of Lewis. “And all of a sudden, he was jealous, and he didn’t want us to hang out together.” Police also spoke with Ellen and Snookie’s cousin Ronald Purdue, who said he received a call from Snookie the morning of her death. “The victim stated to him that she was very depressed and she wanted to get away from her husband, as she was no longer in love with him,” the police report states. “She went on to say that because she was afraid of her husband she was afraid to leave.” Two days after his interview, Ronald called the Rochester Police Department and said he had additional information. A sergeant was dispatched to his residence to interview Ronald and his wife. According to the police report, Ronald said Snookie’s grandmother had asked young Daryl if he knew who hurt his mommy, to which the toddler responded, “Daddy hurt Mommy.” The couple told investigators they didn’t believe any money had been stolen from the house, because Lewis “never left that kind of money around the house for any reason,” according to the police report. They also stated that given the trouble in the relationship, if Snookie “knew the money was in the house she would have taken it and left him.” At the time of Snookie’s death, Lewis was also involved with a woman named Gail Bloodsaw, according to the police report. When she spoke to police in 1975, she told them she had been going out with Lewis since November 1974. The report notes that Gail said Lewis called her three times between 6 p.m. and 10 p.m. on the evening of May 23, 1975. She assumed he was at work because of the machine noise in the background. She also told them he had visited her after work at approximately 12:30 a.m. — around the same time Lewis had placed a call from Kron Street. The police report includes notes from a later interview with Gail Bloodsaw, as well, who the report now described as Lewis’ common-law wife. When she was re-interviewed in 1977, Gail told reporting officers that she had lied to police in her earlier interview and that Lewis had not visited her that night. As she was being interviewed at the station, Lewis arrived and appeared to be “very upset,” according to the report. “Mr. Evans was advised that the Police were just trying to find out who killed his wife & Mr. Evans stated that he did not want the police to do anything regarding the case,” the report states. While at the station, investigators asked Lewis “if he would be willing to speak with Inv. officers about the incident & he refused,” the report notes. During that same 1977 interview, according to the police report, Gail was asked if she had ever forged Snookie’s name on documents, and she replied that she had forged Snookie’s signature during a hospital visit in March 1975 in order to use her health insurance. The police report states that a handwriting expert from the Physical Crimes Unit then examined samples and determined that Gail had also forged Snookie’s signature on a life insurance policy Lewis took out on himself on May 15, 1975, eight days before Snookie’s death. When informed of the finding, Gail said “she believes she may have forged Norris[’s] name to the policy but does not recall doing so,” the report stated. According to the Rochester Police Department, there was not “sufficient evidence to say with certainty the document was forged.” Dateline reached out by phone to Gail Bloodsaw Evans for comment on the events of 1975. She responded, “We have no input on that,” and ended the call. John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Company provided investigators with an explanation of two life insurance policies involving Snookie. Dateline obtained a copy of the letter from the Rochester Police Department. The first policy was one Snookie had taken out on herself in 1971. In 1973, she changed the policy to update it to her married name and changed the beneficiary from her mother to her husband, according to the letter. The second policy was the one Lewis took out on himself on May 15, 1975. The letter stated that policy included “Family Insurance” of $1,250 on each of his children, and $1,000 on his wife. The policy also included “Decreasing Term Insurance on the Insured’s wife in the amount of $10,000 for 25 years.” John Hancock noted Lewis Evans was the beneficiary in the event of the death of his wife. The company, “knowing of no reason why payment should not be made in accordance with the Beneficiary Designation of record, paid the policy proceeds to Mr. Evans,” the letter states. In one of his interviews with police in the days following Snookie’s death, Lewis “denied killing his wife and stated that he spent the entire night, from 3:30PM. to 12:08 AM at work (Roch. Prod.)” According to the report, Lewis’ timecard from Rochester Products shows he clocked in at 3:54 p.m. The report also shows that investigators interviewed Lewis’ supervisor who said he relieved Lewis twice on the night of May 23, 1975: during a meal break at 7:55 until about 8:30 or 8:40 p.m., and again from about 10 to 10:30 p.m. Co-workers interviewed by police reported seeing him playing cards at the plant after 11 p.m. The report notes that Lewis’ timecard shows he clocked out at 12:08 a.m. After speaking with witnesses at the plant, “we cannot implicate Evans as being involved in his wifes [sic] death as we can find no-one to say he left the building,” the police report states. Rochester police interviewed two of Lewis’ male relatives: his half brother Leroy Barnes and their cousin Jessie Martin. The three were very close, Ellen said. Neighbors frequently saw them outside Lewis’ home at 5 Kron Street, according to the case report. Leroy and Jessie were at Lewis’ house the afternoon of May 23, 1975, helping him paint his car, they told police at the time. Jessie told police he walked home when Lewis left for work and stayed there the rest of the night. Leroy said he went to the park until about 7:30 p.m., after which he went to a series of bars and nightclubs, which several alibi witnesses confirmed. Both Leroy and Jessie refused polygraph tests, according to the report. The file also details that a neighbor visited Snookie from about 7:15 to 7:30 p.m., around the same time she called Gina to ask if she wanted to play cards. A different neighbor walked by around 7:45 p.m. and saw Snookie sitting on her front porch. That was the last time anyone reported seeing Snookie alive. Two other neighbors were on a nearby porch from about 11:30 p.m. to 12:15 a.m. Other than Officer Camping’s first arrival, neither of them saw anything out of the ordinary at 5 Kron Street, the police report says. Ellen Evans and Gina Alves told Dateline the family was convinced of Lewis’ involvement. “I don’t know if he physically did it, or there was something that was going on that he had a part in,” Gina said. “But the whole family just felt that.” Decades cold When Snookie’s children, Tamara and Daryl, read the contents of the police report in 2021, they saw their mother’s death in a new light. The siblings told Dateline they had remained in their father’s care, and despite rumors in the extended family, were largely kept in the dark about their mom’s case. “I only knew that she was killed, and that it was someone she knew, because there were no signs of forced entry,” Tamara told Dateline. Both Tamara and Daryl can only remember a handful of times Snookie was mentioned as they were growing up. They also say their father kept them away from their mother’s side of the family. “I rarely heard him speak about her personality as a mother, how she nurtured us, cared for us, or what she was like in daily family life after Daryl and I were born,” Tamara wrote in a follow-up email to Dateline. “I wish I had more of those kinds of memories and stories.” “You hear tidbits of information growing up,” Daryl said. But after reading the police report, he says, everything came together. “I really saw a clear picture of who, what, when, why, where.” Tamara and Daryl told Dateline that after reading through the police report, they called on the Rochester Police Department to look into the case again. It was assigned to Investigator Seth Carr of the Major Crimes Unit in 2022. “The truth is, I kid you not, I walked into Capt. Umbrino’s office, and I told him this case should be on Dateline,” Investigator Carr said. “The kids being involved in trying to figure out what happened to their mother, even with the understanding that that may result in their father being implicated. You know, it’s an interesting dynamic.” Over the next couple of years, Investigator Carr conducted several follow-up interviews, including with Lewis Evans. According to Carr, Lewis gave the same response to every question: “I have nothing to add and nothing to take away.” Carr says he’s considered whether the timing of the 11:24 p.m. anonymous phone call to police could have been intended to steer investigators toward a period when certain people in the case had stronger alibis. “There’s certainly a possibility that that’s not a coincidence,” he said. “That this phone call is made and their alibis are strongest at that time, because maybe the goal is to make the police department believe that the crime occurred at that time.” Considering a time-of-death window wider than the estimated 11:30 p.m. to 12:30 a.m. period opens up new potential scenarios, he added. No one has been charged in connection with the case, and no suspects have been named in Snookie’s death. “It’s fair to say Jessie Martin, Lewis Ev[a]ns and Leroy Barnes (deceased) all remain persons of interest in the case,” Carr said in a follow-up email. When Dateline contacted Lewis Evans about Snookie’s case, he responded: “I don’t know anything about that. Have a good day.” He has declined further calls. Dateline also attempted to contact Jessie Martin for comment. His wife answered the phone and said he was unavailable to speak with us. Dateline asked her to pass along our message, but we have not heard back. The way forward Regarding the case status, Rochester Police Capt. Frank Umbrino and Investigator Carr agree: someone must come forward for the case to progress. Although several forensic samples were pulled from the crime scene — including hair, blood, and fabric — they were not preserved properly to undergo modern forensic testing, Capt. Umbrino told Dateline. “We would need somebody that has direct knowledge of who did the murder, who orchestrated the murder, and they would have to be willing to get up on a stand and testify,” he said. “That’s the only thing that’s going to push this case forward.” Ellen Evans has lived 51 years without her sister. The grief never left. “For years I’d cry,” Ellen said. “Her young life was cut short. She had so much to give.” Tamara Sinclair has lived all but three months of her life without her mother. She says she wakes up every day and thinks about her. She wishes she could call her and tell her about her own children. When asked what justice might look like, Tamara wasn’t sure. “I would have accepted accountability and an apology,” she said. “If the truth could just come out,” Gina Alves said. “I just think that one way or another, you just can’t get away with things.” There is one positive outcome to the siblings’ search for answers. Back in 2021, Gina stumbled across Tamara’s Facebook post asking if anyone knew what happened to her mother. She and Snookie’s cousin separated decades ago, and she hadn’t seen Tamara and Daryl since they were children. After seeing the post, they reconnected. “All these years I’m wondering what happened to Snookie’s babies,” she said. “And then I actually got to see Tiger and I got to see Tammy, and all I could do was just hug them and hug them and hug them.” “I always felt that Snookie was their guardian angel,” she said. “She watched over her babies all these years.” If you have information about the Norris “Snookie” Evans case, you can submit a tip to Rochester NY Unsolved or call the Rochester Police Department’s Major Crimes Unit at 585-428-7157. To leave a tip anonymously, please call Rochester Area Crime Stoppers at 585-423-9300. If you have a story to share with Dateline, please submit it here.
