articles.title: Kaixiao Liu: New Zealand religious sect leader jailed over death of elderly Chinese follower
articles.summary: The body of 70-year-old Shulai Wang was found near a marina in Auckland in 2024.
articles.body:
A New Zealand court has jailed a religious sect leader over the death of an elderly follower who had travelled from China to live with his family.

Kaixiao Liu was found guilty of manslaughter and kidnapping, and sentenced to more than 10 years in prison.

The body of 70-year-old Shulai Wang had been found wrapped in rice bags near Auckland's Gulf Harbour in March 2024, sparking a major homicide investigation which eventually led to Liu.

Liu, a musician who previously appeared in a talent show in China, had denied the charges. He also denied he is a cult leader and said he only attracted followers through his music.

During the trial the court heard that Wang had travelled from Hainan island in China to New Zealand in August 2023.

She moved in with Liu and his family at their house, which Liu had called "the Ark", along with several other female followers.

Prosecutors said that the women acted in "servitude" to Liu and his family, and their lives were tightly controlled by Liu, where they referred to him as "Lord" or "Master".

Wang reportedly spent her days taking care of Liu's children, studying scripture, and planting vegetables.

The court heard that Wang had struggled to comply with the strict rules, possibly due to her old age, and was frequently disciplined.

In March 2024, Wang tried to escape but was caught and restrained. She died later that day, the court heard.

The court heard that Liu, his family, and his followers dumped Wang's body near a marina at Gulf Harbour. Liu had taken his children along for the trip "as camouflage".

The body was found by a fisherman days later. Police eventually traced the rice bags used to wrap Wang's body to Liu, who had made unusually large purchases of that brand of rice.

Besides Liu, his wife, Lanyue Xiao, was sentenced to nearly eight years in jail for kidnapping and manslaughter, amongst other charges. His mother, Xiuyun Li and father, Jingui Liu, had earlier been convicted of kidnapping and misconduct to human remains and are due to be sentenced later this year.

On Tuesday's sentencing, Liu's lawyer asked for leniency arguing that his client feels remorse and "is not a cult leader, nor requires people to follow his cult", according to Radio New Zealand.

New Zealand media outlets reported that Liu had attended a military-based university in China.

In 2011, he was a contestant for China's Got Talent - clips posted online showed him singing onstage blindfolded.

Sometime in 2017, he moved to New Zealand along with Xiao, and the couple became permanent residents.

Liu attracted followers on Chinese social media where he posted religious discussions, video diaries, and clips of himself singing. He also set up a project called Universal Choir that produced cosmic-themed orchestral music.

During the trial a police officer who interviewed one of Liu's female followers gave testimony. He said in court that the woman told him she "met the people over the internet through a song website, and she referred to the occupants of the house as friends".

During the sentencing, Justice Mathew Downs said Liu had shown "callous indifference" towards Wang.

"Because of you, Ms Wang died a lonely, frightening death. You display no remorse whatsoever. You should feel shame."

articles.title: 'Haven't achieved 1% of my success': Kangana Ranaut slams critics, targets Baba Ramdev over comments on women
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: BJP MP and actor Kangana Ranaut on Monday hit back at several film industry figures and yoga guru Baba Ramdev over their criticism of her r.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP MP and actor Kangana Ranaut on Monday hit back at several film industry figures and yoga guru Baba Ramdev over their criticism of her recent remarks, accusing her detractors of targeting her for publicity.Speaking to reporters at Delhi Airport, Ranaut said she would not take advice from people who, according to her, had not achieved comparable professional success.âEvery day, I see people like Ashutosh Rana â who says I bark like a dog â or the likes of Sonu Sood. Then there are people like Rakhi Sawant, who make all sorts of remarks about my character, and Taapsee Pannu, who insults my parents, my upbringing and my background,â she said.Ranaut described her critics as âfailedâ and âcompletely irrelevantâ people who, she alleged, abuse her to gain media attention.âIf you haven't achieved even one per cent of the success I have in life, I am not going to listen to you,â she said, adding that she would not tolerate what she called personal attacks.Ranaut also hit out at Baba Ramdev over his remarks on women, saying he had âcrossed every boundary of decencyâ.âThe kind of comments he has made about a woman have shamed society. Given the remarks he makes about women, I think he really needs to reflect on his perspective regarding them,â she said.The latest exchange follows the controversy over Ranaut's âGeneration Gutterâ remark while criticising protesters at Jantar Mantar. Her comments triggered criticism from several public figures, including Sonu Sood and Rakhi Sawant.The controversy also brought her longstanding differences with actors Taapsee Pannu and Ashutosh Rana into focus. Ramdev had separately criticised Ranaut's remarks about the younger generation, leading to a public exchange between the two.Ranaut, who represents Himachal Pradesh's Mandi Lok Sabha constituency, has frequently been involved in public disagreements with personalities from the film industry and other public figures.(With ANI inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: London in drought: 'We need to change how we think about water'
articles.summary: Experts say a changing climate and increasing demand for water will mean people need to make changes.
articles.body:
Hyde Park looks more like the Serengeti and the green belt has turned yellow. But with London now seeing the occasional shower, does that mean we are no longer in drought? And if not, the big question is how long will the drought last?

The capital is particularly susceptible to drought as there is a very large population, in an area that is actually very dry. Experts call it "water stressed."

The myth is London is a rainy city, yet the capital gets less rain than many other cities in Europe.

According to the Met Office the Thames Valley, London and the north Kent coast normally receive less than 650mm (26in) of rain every year. By comparison, Rome gets up to 900mm (35in).

SES Water covers parts of Surrey, Kent and south London and at the moment it is one of the few water companies that doesn't have a hosepipe ban.

Daniel Kennedy, the firm's water services director, says it is impossible to predict when the drought will end.

"We do model our position with where we think things might go, but a lot of it is determined by the hot weather and the prolonged dry period that we've had."

He says water companies "are looking forward to when the rain does come because it does ease the position somewhat. But until it happens, it's really difficult to say how long it'll go on for.

"We would want a sustained period of rain... so we can replenish our groundwater stocks and our reservoirs, to enable us to have water in supply in our reserves for next year."

Liz Stephens is a professor in climate risks and resilience at the University of Reading.

She thinks it could take months to get back to normal, noting that previous hosepipe bans in parts of the South East were only lifted "towards the end of January, early February", while "the Thames Water hosepipe ban lifted towards the end of November".

"It really does depend on the amount of rainfall that we get. If we see a dry autumn and winter, and we don't see that recharge of groundwater, the rise in reservoir levels, potentially we could be looking at similar restrictions next summer as well," she says.

There is even a possibility this drought might not come to an end this year, according to Stephens.

"If we don't get the amount of rain that's needed, then there will be a lot of concern about the water supply going into next spring and summer as well. We probably would then expect further restrictions.

"The 1976 drought came after a period of low winter rainfall as well. And in that situation that summer there were the standpipes on the streets for water supply," she says.

Most of the capital's water comes from chalk aquifers under the ground. These take much longer to recharge than reservoirs.

Stephens also points out that while water companies may have been preparing for a prolonged drought, they are now facing other issues as well.

"They might not have been able to anticipate the type of demands that we're now seeing in the South East, not just from the increase in population, but also the very recent increase in data centres and the demand that they're putting on water as well."

Reservoir levels are currently at about 70%, which is lower than usual at this time of year.

Martin Padley, water director at Thames Water, which does have a hosepipe ban , says the company is grateful to everyone for reducing their water use, but given the current situation "we're asking customers to keep going and continue using only what they need.

"Small changes, such as taking shorter showers, turning off taps and avoiding non-essential water use outdoors, all help reduce pressure on our network while our teams continue working around the clock to find and fix leaks."

More than two-thirds of England now in drought

Keeping London's canal boats afloat during drought

Looking down on London's straw-coloured parks

Long-term water scarcity is becoming more of an issue in London and the South East.

No major reservoirs have been completed in England since 1992. But a growing population and developments like new data centres are putting intense pressure on our water supplies.

Also, climate change is bringing hotter, drier summers that increase the risk of drought.

The government's solution is to build nine new reservoirs by 2050, potentially providing 670 million litres of extra water daily.

But some experts say we're thinking about water all wrong.

Hannah Cloke, professor of hydrology at the School of Archaeology, Geography and Environmental Science at the University of Reading, believes "we need a complete overhaul of the way we use water".

"We need to plug leaks, cut down on waste and use water more than once in our homes and buildings before sloshing it down the drain. We need to catch more water wherever it falls – not just in the river basins that are linked to big reservoirs," she says.

"An unprecedented climate calls for unprecedented solutions," adds Cloke.

"These could include the widespread roll out of sustainable drainage solutions that mimic nature and capture rainwater where it falls, on roofs or ditches filled with plants, rather than letting it rush straight down the drains into the rivers."

And one of the big unknowns long term is data centres.

Stephens says they're making an enormous difference.

"Thames Water had been trying to predict demand over the next 10 years... They've estimated that about 30% of that increased demand is coming from the growth of data centres.

"And I think they've already admitted that they're underestimating the demand that's happened so far from those data centres. It's an incredible amount of water that these centres use."

A huge new reservoir is planned to be built in Oxfordshire, called the White Horse Reservoir , to improve water supply.

However, Stephens says that while it will cover "a very large area of land, actually, by the time it's built, it might already be out of date.

"The extra volume that it's going to supply is roughly equivalent to that sort of upper estimate of the demand from data centres. So these really are crazy amounts of water that these data centres can use."

Kennedy, from SES Water, says we will have to use water wisely throughout the year, especially with a changing climate.

This includes the likes of having shorter showers, turning the tap off when cleaning your teeth and making sure washing machines and dishwashers are only run when they are fully loaded, he says.

"If we can use water wisely all year round, it will obviously help us with our stocks in the times of the year when we really need it.

"The world is changing and we've had five heatwaves already this summer. So people are starting to understand that water is a precious commodity," he says.

At the moment, about 20% of water is lost through leaks. Thames Water says it is investing a record amount £21bn in fixing them. Critics say that is too little, too late.

Thames Water has also estimated that it could face a daily shortfall of over one billion litres of water by 2050. The funding needed for improvements and new water systems will be significant.

Its proposals include the new reservoir in Oxfordshire and a water recycling project in west London at Teddington. Both have faced opposition.

To match the demand, Thames Water is also striving to reduce daily water use to 110 litres per person by 2050, with current water use in the area at about 140 litres per person.

In other words, all of us will have to use less water.

In the face of a hotter climate, the mayor of London has created a heat plan, called Heat Ready London , which also highlights behaviour change as crucial.

It says: "Alongside infrastructure upgrades, changes in behaviours and system operation are essential to reduce pressure on water supplies.

"To enhance long-term water security, investment should be scaled up through a portfolio-based and integrated water management approach, recognising that no single intervention can address future challenges in isolation.

"A balanced portfolio of measures – including smart meters, active leakage reduction, water-efficiency initiatives, water recycling and reuse, rainwater harvesting, and targeted new supply schemes – should be implemented in a co-ordinated manner to deliver greater resilience and adaptability across the entire water system."

Experts say the whole water system needs a rethink to make it fit for the future.

Certainly, with a warming climate this won't be the last hosepipe ban in London and the South East.

articles.title: Silver prices today, Tuesday, August 25, 2026: Silver prices pull back slightly, but remain over $68
articles.summary: Silver (SI=F) September futures opened at $68.96 per ounce on Tuesday, August 25, 2026, up 0.5% from Monday's closing price. Silver fell this morning to $68....
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

Silver ( SI=F ) September futures opened at $68.96 per ounce on Tuesday, August 25, 2026 , up 0.5% from Monday's closing price. Silver fell slightly this morning to $68.07 as of 8:08 a.m. ET.

Silver prices are pulling back slightly this morning, despite holding onto weekly and monthly gains of 5.7% and 17.6%, respectively.

Most investors are looking ahead to tomorrow's inflation report, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index, and the Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's speech on Friday at Jackson Hole.

Inflation concerns and their impact on the Fed's decision to potentially raise rates following its September meeting continue to be a focal point for silver investors, as higher rates are a natural headwind for silver prices since the precious metal doesn't pay interest.

The opening price of silver futures on Tuesday, August 25, 2026 , was 0.5% higher compared to Monday's closing price. Here's how today's opening silver price has changed versus last week, month, and year:

For context, silver's year-over-year growth was 173.3% on May 14.

24/7 silver price tracking: Don't forget you can monitor the current price of silver on Yahoo Finance 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

Want to learn more about the current top-performing companies in the silver industry? Explore a list of the top-performing companies in the silver industry using the Yahoo Finance Screener . You can create your own screeners with over 150 different screening criteria.

Silver price predictions for the next decade

Silver price forecasts vary wildly by expert. Some say silver's price will hold steady or experience modest growth, while others predict huge price spikes. Here are some of the biggest predictions for silver's price:

Experts with BlackRock and J.P. Morgan agree that the outlook for silver remains strong, and its price will increase. By the end of 2026, experts predict silver's price will surpass $80 per ounce, and it could reach $100 per ounce by 2030.

Does that mean you should buy lots of silver? Be aware that predictions can change, and they may revise their forecasts at any time.

With the conflict in the Middle East, investors are increasingly concerned about economic turmoil and manufacturing supply chain disruptions. Historically, that means investors will increasingly buy precious metals, such as silver.

Because buying an ounce of gold is prohibitively expensive for new investors, silver coins or bars are a more accessible entry point, so there may be increased demand.

Compared to gold, silver's price tends to be more volatile, with more rises and falls. Its price fluctuates due to changes in industrial demand and investor confidence.

For example, at the beginning of January 2026, silver's price topped $113 per ounce. But by February, its price dropped to $77 per ounce, a decrease of about 32% in just a few weeks.

articles.title: Father's house was rammed by car before son died in A66 crash
articles.summary: The house belonging to Cole Worthy's father is significantly damaged and its windows are smashed.
articles.body:
A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.

Cole Worthy, 17, was one of five young men who died when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle, also killing two police officers.

Before the crash at 03:39 BST on Saturday, police had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 was seen ramming properties.

The BBC understands that, after his father's home was rammed, Worthy and the four others set out in the Passat. Police said they were linking the activities of the Volvo XC60 and the Passat.

There is no suggestion Worthy's father was involved in criminal activity.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash , as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Worthy.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.

The rammed house is a red bricked semi-detached that sits in a quiet residential street in Acklam.

The downstairs bay window has been smashed, with bricks scattered beneath it, and an upstairs bedroom window has also been broken.

Neighbours, who did not want to be identified, said Worthy sometimes stayed at his father's property.

Locals described hearing loud bangs at around two in the morning on Saturday and said the street had been full of police all weekend.

Meanwhile, nine men and three women, aged between 18 and 61, were arrested across Teesside on Monday as part of the investigation into the lead-up to the crash. They were held on a range of offences, including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.

Kai Beattie, of Foxrush Court, Redcar, has been charged with possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.

Cameron George, of Micklow Close, Redcar, has been charged with possession of class A and class B drugs with intent to supply, and possession of criminal property.

Cleveland Police said on Tuesday that five further arrests had been made, including a 16-year-old boy and two men, 18 and 21, who were held on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group.

A 55-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender and a 23-year-old man on suspicion of making threats to kill.

Those previously arrested as part of the investigation are:

Three men, aged 24, 19 and 35, all held on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group and possession of an offensive weapon. They are in police custody.

A man, 21, held on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, possession of an offensive weapon and criminal damage. He has been remanded on recall to prison

A 30-year-old woman arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender and who is in police custody

A 20-year-old man arrested on suspicion of threats to cause criminal damage and public order. He remains in custody

A 26-year-old man was charged with possession with intent to supply class A drugs, as well as the possession of criminal property. He was remanded in custody ahead of his next court hearing

Another man, 39, and a 47-year-old woman have been released on conditional bail after both being arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate, possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs, and possession of class C drugs

An 18-year-old man has been released on unconditional bail after being arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate, possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs, and possession of class C drugs

A 61-year-old woman has been released on conditional bail after being arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate

paragraphs: A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.
Cole Worthy, 17, was one of five young men who died when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle, also killing two police officers.
Before the crash at 03:39 BST on Saturday, police had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 was seen ramming properties.
The BBC understands that, after his father's home was rammed, Worthy and the four others set out in the Passat. Police said they were linking the activities of the Volvo XC60 and the Passat.
There is no suggestion Worthy's father was involved in criminal activity.
PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash , as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Worthy.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.
Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.
The rammed house is a red bricked semi-detached that sits in a quiet residential street in Acklam.
The downstairs bay window has been smashed, with bricks scattered beneath it, and an upstairs bedroom window has also been broken.
Neighbours, who did not want to be identified, said Worthy sometimes stayed at his father's property.
Locals described hearing loud bangs at around two in the morning on Saturday and said the street had been full of police all weekend.

Meanwhile, nine men and three women, aged between 18 and 61, were arrested across Teesside on Monday as part of the investigation into the lead-up to the crash. They were held on a range of offences, including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.
Kai Beattie, of Foxrush Court, Redcar, has been charged with possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.
Cameron George, of Micklow Close, Redcar, has been charged with possession of class A and class B drugs with intent to supply, and possession of criminal property.
Cleveland Police said on Tuesday that five further arrests had been made, including a 16-year-old boy and two men, 18 and 21, who were held on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group.
A 55-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender and a 23-year-old man on suspicion of making threats to kill.

Three men, aged 24, 19 and 35, all held on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group and possession of an offensive weapon. They are in police custody.
A man, 21, held on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, possession of an offensive weapon and criminal damage. He has been remanded on recall to prison
A 30-year-old woman arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender and who is in police custody
A 20-year-old man arrested on suspicion of threats to cause criminal damage and public order. He remains in custody
A 26-year-old man was charged with possession with intent to supply class A drugs, as well as the possession of criminal property. He was remanded in custody ahead of his next court hearing

articles.title: IShowSpeedâs $10,000 challenge goes viral after participant lifts 20kg cube in under 5 minutes
articles.summary: US Streamers News: IShowSpeedâs $10,000 challenge quickly turned into a surprise moment after a participant managed to lift a heavy 20kg cube in less than five minutes. .
articles.body: IShowSpeedâs $10,000 challenge quickly turned into a surprise moment after a participant managed to lift a heavy 20kg cube in less than five minutes. The popular streamer had set up a simple public challenge: anyone who could lift the cube could win $10,000. The metal cube weighed about 45 pounds and had no handle, making it much harder to grab than a normal weight. Several people tried and failed, including some strong-looking contestants. However, one young participant stepped up and completed the challenge almost immediately.IShowSpeedâs $10,000 cube challenge ends in just minutesThe challenge looked simple at first. A large metal cube was placed on the ground, and a sign offered $10,000 to anyone who could lift it.The cube weighed around 20 kilograms, or about 45 pounds. But it did not have a handle, bar, or any grooves to hold. Contestants had to use just their hand to grab the smooth cube and lift it from the ground.Several people gave it a try but could not complete the challenge. Some of the contestants were bigger and looked strong enough to lift the weight. Still, the shape of the cube made the task much harder.Then, within the first five minutes, a young participant stepped forward.He grabbed the cube with one hand and pulled it up from the ground. As the cube came higher, he moved his hand underneath it and pulled it closer to his body. He kept control of the weight and did not drop it.The lift was complete, meaning he had earned the $10,000 prize.IShowSpeed stunned by participantâs unusual method to lift 20kg cubeIShowSpeed appeared shocked when the participant completed the challenge so quickly. He even asked people around him if the attempt should count.The short discussion was about how the participant lifted the cube. Some viewers felt that moving his palm underneath the cube made the lift easier than simply pinching the cube with his fingers.However, the challenge only appeared to require contestants to âlift the cube.â There was no clear rule saying that the participant could not move his hand underneath it.Speed and his team eventually accepted the attempt and declared the participant the winner. Speed then ran over to celebrate with him.The challenge also showed why a 20kg cube can feel much harder than a 20kg dumbbell. A dumbbell has a handle that makes it easy to hold. A smooth cube gives your fingers very little to grab.Grip strength, hand size, finger length, and even sweat can make a big difference when trying to lift something like this.In the end, what looked like a difficult $10,000 challenge lasted only a few minutes. The unexpected win quickly became the main talking point among viewers, while the debate over the lifting method continued online.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: UK PM Andy Burnham likely to meet Trump at UN summit amid Ukraine missile plea
articles.summary: UK News: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to travel to New York next month for the UN General Assembly, possibly setting up a face-to-face meeti.
articles.body: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to travel to New York next month for the UN General Assembly, possibly setting up a face-to-face meeting with US President Donald Trump as London seeks stronger international support for Ukraine.Burnham told Bloomberg in an interview that he was âlooking forward to going to New York in Septemberâ, although Downing Street said plans for the trip had not yet been finalised. The UN General Assembly is scheduled to take place from September 22 to 28.First US visit since taking officeThe visit, if confirmed, would be Burnhamâs first trip to the US since becoming prime minister in July. It would also allow him to meet Trump and other world leaders during the annual gathering in New York.The timing could prove challenging, however, as the Labour Partyâs annual conference begins in Liverpool on September 27.Burnhamâs remarks came during his first official overseas visit as prime minister, to Kyiv, where he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and reiterated Britainâs support for Ukraine.Burnham urges allies to send more PatriotsDuring his Ukraine visit, Burnham urged Kyivâs allies to provide more Patriot interceptor missiles as Ukraine faces intensified Russian missile attacks.Zelenskyy has repeatedly called for additional US-made Patriot missiles, with supplies to Ukraine falling as some interceptors have been redirected to the Middle East following the outbreak of the US-Iran war.Burnham told Bloomberg he was âreally confidentâ the shortage could be resolved, but said it would require negotiations involving several countries.âThere are other players who could help in the mix who we have influence with,â he said, adding that a solution would likely involve âa lot of layers and a lot of negotiationâ.UK to share missile technology with UkraineDuring his Kyiv visit, Burnham announced that Britain would allow defence company MBDA to declassify information about UK-made components used in the Storm Shadow/SCALP long-range missiles.The move is intended to help Ukraine develop its own version of the missile as it continues to defend itself against Russian attacks.Burnham also co-chaired a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, telling participating nations they were doing âeverything we canâ to use their own stocks and encourage others to provide weapons to Ukraine.Russia has intensified ballistic missile attacks amid Ukraineâs shortage of air-defence interceptors, with at least 23 people reportedly killed and more than 100 wounded over the past three days.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Dozens of new wildfires break out across Greece
articles.summary: Thirty-nine new wildfires have broken out across Greece within the space of a few hours, the fire service reported on Tuesday. The most severe fire is raging...
articles.body:
Thirty-nine new wildfires have broken out across Greece within the space of a few hours, the fire service reported on Tuesday.

The most severe fire is raging on the island of Salamis, off the coast of Athens, according to firefighters.

The island is home to the Greek Navy's largest base. According to firefighters on the ground, the base was not at risk.

The fire raged through a gorge and was tackled by numerous firefighting aircraft and helicopters. In addition, large fire brigade units and volunteers have been deployed, broadcaster ERT reported.

Due to the ongoing drought, the risk of wildfires remains high across large parts of Greece, according to the civil defence agency.

Temperatures in central Athens reached 40 degrees Celsius on Tuesday and the current heatwave has been forecast to persist until the beginning of next week.

articles.title: Beyond China's humanoid robots, a quieter machine revolution is unfolding
articles.summary: There are more than two million robots working in China's factories - and they are scaling up fast.
articles.body:
Watch: BBC visits factories in China with robot workers

"I take a nap and the world changes," says Chen Tianyu.

His world certainly does. The 28-year-old keeps up with the latest technology by spending his spare time in factories that are switching to automation. That way he knows what to prioritise when teaching his class about artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics.

In front of him, around 30 college students are studying code. One of them is typing furiously as his eyes dart from the screen to the robot: "The idea is it will grab that cylindrical piece and move it over there."

A line of industrial robots are waiting to be programmed, and in another part of the classroom, students are trying to develop robotic medical instruments. As he guides them, Chen declares: "If you are not needed by the world of AI and robotics, then you'll definitely be among those eliminated".

For the people in this room, this is a step - or rather a leap - towards a future that China is meticulously building: Xi Jinping's $20bn (£14.7bn) plan to put his country at the forefront of innovation and in direct competition with the US.

The evidence is all around them. They are in the Hangzhou Technician Institute, one of several huge, purpose-built vocational schools that want to churn out the next generation of tech-savvy engineers. The campus sits on the outskirts of Hangzhou, a former imperial capital whose futuristic skyline is just the first hint of its role as a global tech hub.

Across the country, there are more than two million robots working in China's factories - which is more than anywhere else - and they are continuing to scale up at extraordinary speed.

It is a commitment that will surely change the world, much like the last time the Chinese economy underwent a massive transformation. It is already shipping its robots across the globe: more than half of the world's industrial robots are now made in China.

What is less clear is the impact of such sweeping automation in a country that sits at the heart of global manufacturing, trade and innovation. What does this mean for China's human workforce, for instance? And how would we be able to truly measure the cost of this transformation in a regime that controls information so tightly?

The future of China's workers is uncertain in the industrial revolution the world has been watching: gleaming solar grids, peak hours made noiseless by electric vehicles, machines that run faster than Usain Bolt. Over the weekend, China hosted the second edition of the World Humanoid Games where robots boxed, sprinted and marched.

What is fuelling this spectacle is another, less visible revolution happening inside factories and classrooms.

The BBC has visited industrial sites where we have been shown robots that do not look human, or dance or leap on stage but weld, paint, lift, assemble and work around the clock without a break or benefits. Some are designed to build more robots. We have also been inside academies where China is training the people who will work alongside its robotic workforce.

This is a front-row seat to what Xi calls China's "new productive forces" - and how they could reshape the country.

On a factory floor in the southern city of Chengdu, the old and and the new are working side by side.

An assembly line of around 30 middle-aged men and women is screwing, drilling and polishing CRP Technology's signature product: a robotic arm which performs various industrial tasks. Also in the room are four young engineers crowded around a console, trying to crack the code for a prototype, a new robot that they hope will help build other robots.

One of them, 31-year-old Pang Kai, who is part of the research and development team, pushes the sleek skeleton across the room. Because China's future workforce is not quite ready to strut out. For now, it can only do simple repetitive movements, such as scan a QR code.

"Maybe in another half year, it can do another task," Pang says, smiling wistfully. It's a long road and the team are celebrating every small win.

CRP Technology, which employs around 300 people, has been building robot arms for nine years. Each arm can be tailored to a factory's needs to help build cars, electronics or wind turbines. The firm says a single arm can be programmed to perform more than 90% of repetitive tasks.

The engineers also wonder if, one day, they can replace the company's workforce. "We want our new robot to be like human beings. We hope it can think by itself," says Pang. "We need these kinds of robots because maybe in 10 years, we won't have enough workers in China."

A shrinking population and an ageing workforce is another reason Beijing is in a hurry to revolutionise its factories. By 2035, more than a third of China's population will be over 60, according to official estimates. The country will also lose nearly 60 million people in the next decade - almost equivalent to the population of France - according to some estimates.

The hope is that increased automation will fill this looming gap in the workforce before it starts to affect an already sluggish economy. But the speed of the transition is key. Around 120 million people still work in the manufacturing sector. If China moves too quickly, job losses could follow dealing a catastrophic blow to millions who depend on factory wages.

"In theory, machines can work 24 hours a day, which is certainly an advantage compared with human workers. But machines also require maintenance. Every day we need time for that, and each month the production line also requires inspection and repair," says Cao Li, vice-president of EV maker Leapmotor.

Increasingly popular in Europe and the UK, the company's budget-friendly, tech-focused cars come together at the Hangzhou factory with robots aiding the process at every step. At the end of the assembly line, more humans emerge.

The company has more than 25,000 workers and hundreds of them make the final checks as the sparkling new vehicles roll past. Will there be a day when they are no longer needed?

"It's entirely possible," Cao says. "And it may come relatively quickly. In workshops, including stamping, welding, and painting, we've basically achieved 100% automation."

China has the edge over the US due to its enormous manufacturing base. Motors, batteries, electronics, gears, sensors - everything needed to build the body of a robot is all at hand.

"China also has an idea. It has a plan. They know where they want to be in five years. They plan at a top level, but they break it down to the regions, to the municipalities," says Dr Susanne Bieller, General Secretary of the International Federation of Robotics.

"If you want to build a robot in Shenzhen - there's an entire ecosystem. It takes you less than one hour to source the components you need to make a robot. In Europe it can take you up to a week."

However, she acknowledges that while China is good at building the body, the US is still leading at building the "brain", which includes developing the AI to programme robots. And yet Chinese firms, from DeepSeek to Moonshot, have been unveiling new AI models that they say can compete with top US firms.

Driven by an "open-source" approach, where AI start-ups share their code, Chinese innovation has been able to catch up faster than expected, despite US export controls over critical advanced chips. Analysts now believe that the next leg of this race will be determined not by who has the best language model, but who can put this intelligence into millions of machines.

And that is why China is also investing in producing a generation of students learning to imagine what could come next.

At the Hangzhou Technician Institute, for example, children can start from the age of 15. And the scale of what is being taught can feel staggering. There is an entire building dedicated to engines and aeronautics, and a restricted floor for students who will work to keep China at the forefront of processing rare earths - another crucial commodity in the battle with Washington.

Some see this as a solution to China's stubbornly high youth unemployment rate, with one in five struggling to find a job. "Our students are in demand and can even be pre-booked by companies. They don't need to worry about employment at all, and we hold competitions as part of their training," Chen, the young teacher, says.

"It's better to find your position within the technological wave. In the process of progress, structural changes are bound to occur, and these structural changes are exactly where students' future employment opportunities lie."

But China still faces serious economic challenges, from a property crisis that continues to drag on to huge local government debt and persistently low consumption.

It is unclear if and how the revolution Beijing is touting will fix these, and it is hard to gauge how those whose jobs are threatened feel about the change that is coming. Will robots create prosperity for them, or simply take many of their jobs?

"My students ask me what will happen in the future," Chen says. "I say I don't know. Technology is changing so fast. But we can't just stand still and sleep here. We have to move forward to see what we are capable of doing."

And yet Chinese firms, from DeepSeek to Moonshot, have been unveiling new AI models that they say can compete with top US firms.

Driven by an "open-source" approach, where AI start-ups share their code, Chinese innovation has been able to catch up faster than expected, despite US export controls over critical advanced chips. Analysts now believe that the next leg of this race will be determined not by who has the best language model, but who can put this intelligence into millions of machines.
And that is why China is also investing in producing a generation of students learning to imagine what could come next.

At the Hangzhou Technician Institute, for example, children can start from the age of 15. And the scale of what is being taught can feel staggering. There is an entire building dedicated to engines and aeronautics, and a restricted floor for students who will work to keep China at the forefront of processing rare earths - another crucial commodity in the battle with Washington.

Some see this as a solution to China's stubbornly high youth unemployment rate, with one in five struggling to find a job. "Our students are in demand and can even be pre-booked by companies. They don't need to worry about employment at all, and we hold competitions as part of their training," Chen, the young teacher, says.

"It's better to find your position within the technological wave. In the process of progress, structural changes are bound to occur, and these structural changes are exactly where students' future employment opportunities lie."
But China still faces serious economic challenges, from a property crisis that continues to drag on to huge local government debt and persistently low consumption.

It is unclear if and how the revolution Beijing is touting will fix these, and it is hard to gauge how those whose jobs are threatened feel about the change that is coming. Will robots create prosperity for them, or simply take many of their jobs?

"My students ask me what will happen in the future," Chen says. "I say I don't know. Technology is changing so fast. But we can't just stand still and sleep here. We have to move forward to see what we are capable of doing."

articles.title: Pakistan, Iran made ‘significant progress’ to end US-Iran war, minister says
articles.summary: Pakistan and Iran on Tuesday announced that “significant progress” has been made toward ending the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran, according to Pakistan’s interior...
articles.body:
Pakistan and Iran on Tuesday announced that "significant progress" has been made toward ending the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran, according to Pakistan's interior minister, Reuters reported .

Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pakistan's army chief, met with Iranian officials in Tehran about measures to prevent the conflict from growing and to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which has been closed under Iranian control, causing gas prices to skyrocket.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who traveled with Munir, said their meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was "very positive and productive."

"The Iranian President candidly shared his Government's perspective and concerns, and we had a very constructive exchange on the issues involved," Naqvi wrote on the social platform X . "Significant progress was made, and the meeting concluded on a highly positive note. We remain hopeful that this momentum will help pave the way for further progress and lasting peace in the region."

Naqvi said the discussion focused on the conflict and a path forward for the region. He added that they talked about the steps needed to restore the interim peace deal signed by the U.S. and Iran in June, which expired last week.

Munir called President Trump ahead of the talks in Tehran, Reuters reported.

The Pakistani delegation's visit comes as Iran and Oman announced a plan to allow navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and clear mines placed in the waterway. Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi met with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in Tehran about a "phased framework" for the strait.

"The proposed framework includes the establishment of a joint temporary navigational corridor through the Strait of Hormuz and an agreement to implement a joint project to clear the Strait of mines," Oman's Foreign Ministry posted on the social platform X .

Talks regarding the strait's future would include an agreement on "a mechanism for information-sharing, traffic management, and the provision of relevant navigational and security services."

"In this context, both sides underscored the importance of convening joint discussions with regional states bordering the waters of the Gulf," the foreign minister's office added. "They further stressed the need to uphold applicable international law and respect the sovereign rights of the coastal states."

Trump previously threatened Oman over potentially striking a deal with Iran, warning the country that "we'll bomb the s--- out of them" if it "gets in the way."

Iranian officials have insisted that the strait will reopen after Trump withdraws a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, pays compensation for damages from the war, lifts sanctions and unfreezes assets.

The Trump administration has also warned other countries that they could face economic consequences if they do not cut off their financial ties to the Iranian regime. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday announced " Operation Economic Outcast ," a new campaign to constrict Iran's economy, but offered few specific details.

"Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior, why would I want to blow up the global financial system?" Bessent said in response to a reporter's question about the operation's details.

articles.title: Thousands of dragonflies are suddenly swarming across California, and the insects could help farmers control crop pests naturally
articles.summary: US News: California is seeing an unusual surge in dragonflies, with large groups appearing over parks, ponds and farms after warm spring and early summer rain..
articles.body: California is seeing an unusual surge in dragonflies, with large groups appearing over parks, ponds and farms after warm spring and early summer rain. The insects have been especially noticeable around the San Francisco Bay Area, where residents have reported seeing dozens flying together. Oakland nursery owner Peter Veilleux even counted about 100 dragonflies in one group while walking his dog near Lake Merritt. The sudden appearance may look mysterious, but experts say weather conditions probably created the right opportunity for the insects to spread. According to The Associated Press(AP), dragonfly expert Kathy Biggs believes warm monsoon storms helped drive the increase, with many of the insects likely being âwandering gliders,â a migratory species capable of travelling long distances. For Californians, the spectacle is not only striking but also useful, because these natural predators feed on mosquitoes and crop pests.Warm spring rains triggering huge dragonfly swarmsKathy Biggs, a dragonfly expert and co-author of âDragonflies of California,â told AP that unusually warm monsoon storms moved through the state during late spring and early summer. Those conditions appear to have helped produce the huge number now being seen. Many of the dragonflies are probably wandering gliders. Unlike species that remain close to the water where they emerge, wandering gliders are highly migratory and can turn up in large numbers when weather conditions are favourable. The insects can travel long distances by taking advantage of changes in air pressure. Biggs described their movement as effectively âsurfingâ the pressure systems created by the monsoon weather. They can reach speeds of about 35 mph (56 kph), allowing them to cover considerable distances. That explains why people in different parts of California can suddenly encounter large swarms of dragonflies. The insects do not necessarily remain in one location for long. Biggs said migratory species can stay somewhere for only a few days before moving on.What dragonflies are doing around farms in CaliforniaThe swarms are more than an unusual summer sight. They are also providing farmers with a natural form of pest control. AP reported that Joe Del Bosque, who farms in Fresno County noticed unusually large numbers of dragonflies flying about 10 to 20 feet (3 to 6 metres) above him earlier in August. Dragonflies are welcome visitors on his farm because they prey on insects that can damage crops. Del Bosque said the dragonflies feed on aphids, whiteflies and fruit flies, while also catching larger flying insects such as adult aphids and moths. He compared the insects to tiny fighter jets because of the way they rapidly chase and capture prey in mid-air. Ladybirds also help control pests around the crops, but dragonflies bring a different advantage by targeting insects while they are flying.Why are dragonflies such effective huntersDragonflies are remarkably efficient predators. Chris Grinter, senior collection manager of entomology at the California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco, said that their strong flight muscles, excellent vision and agility make them particularly effective hunters. More than 90% of their hunting attempts are successful. He also said a dragonfly can eat hundreds of mosquitoes in a single day. That makes the sudden California swarms potentially beneficial for people as well as farms. California has about 70 species of dragonflies, although most are not migratory. Many remain close to the places where they emerge. The wandering gliders responsible for much of the current spectacle are different because they can travel with changing weather systems.Life cycle of dragonfliesThe swarms seen above California are only the brief flying stage of a much longer life cycle. Dragonflies spend most of their lives underwater. After mating, females lay tiny eggs in freshwater. Once the eggs hatch, the young insects, known as nymphs, remain underwater and hunt other small creatures. According to AP, this underwater stage can last at least six months and, for some species, as long as five years. During that time, nymphs can feed on mosquito larvae, tadpoles and even other dragonfly nymphs. Eventually, they emerge from the water, shed their skin and become the familiar four-winged insects seen around ponds and fields. Their wings can move independently, allowing them to fly forwards, backwards, upwards and downwards and even hover in place. Once airborne, however, their lives are relatively short. Adults may survive for only a few weeks or months, spending that time hunting, moving between freshwater habitats and reproducing.People who enjoy watching dragonflies can make their gardens more welcoming to them. Biggs recommends avoiding pesticides and creating fish-free ponds where dragonflies can reproduce. Sunny areas with places for the insects to perch can also provide suitable conditions. Such spaces can offer dragonflies somewhere to rest while giving them access to the small insects they hunt. The sight nevertheless offers a reminder of how quickly insects can respond when weather, water and food come together.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Australian officials allege 3M knew for 50 years its firefighting products were toxic
articles.summary: The government alleges internal company documents discussed the chemicals' ability to remain in the human body.
articles.body:
Australia's federal government says U.S. manufacturing conglomerate 3M kept selling firefighting foam for decades even though the company allegedly knew the chemicals in it could harm people, animals, and the environment.

Those allegations appear in extensive federal court papers tied to Australia's lawsuit seeking more than 2 billion Australian dollars ($1.4 billion) from 3M and its Australian subsidiary, according to The Guardian .

The accusations add to growing scrutiny of corporate decisions that can leave communities grappling with pollution long after the products themselves are gone.

Attorney General Michelle Rowland confirmed that the government was taking 3M to court over PFAS pollution connected to 28 defense bases in Australia, The Guardian reported.

The government says 3M sold aqueous film-forming foam, or AFFF, that contained PFAS "forever chemicals," which then polluted soil and water and led to major environmental and economic harm.

The court papers argue that by 1973, 3M and its Australian operations should already have understood that the products posed potential dangers.

The government alleges internal company documents discussed toxicity and the chemicals' ability to remain in the human body and also raised possible concerns about kidney function, the immune system, fertility, puberty, and infant birth weight.

The filing says that when defense personnel watched product demonstrations in 1967 and 1968, company brochures still described the foam as "non-toxic," The Guardian reported.

3M also said the products were "non-irritating" to humans, would not damage grass, were biodegradable, and were "not expected to adversely affect the ecology of receiving streams in the vicinity of [their] use."

If the government's claims are upheld, it would mean the company continued to promote a hazardous product in reassuring terms even as contamination risks spread into everyday places such as groundwater, drains, and nearby land.

PFAS are used in a wide range of industrial and household products because they resist heat, grease, and water.

However, those same qualities also make them incredibly persistent in every sense.

Many do not break down easily, which is why they are often referred to as forever chemicals.

Australia banned three key PFAS chemicals in 2025 after years of concern over health risks and environmental contamination.

One of them, PFOA, has been identified as cancer-causing in humans.

The filing says affected sites have required contaminated soil to be removed and treated, and investigations around the bases have been underway since about 2011.

When companies describe products as safe or eco-friendly while concealing environmental concerns, the fallout can last for generations, part of a broader deceptive business practice known as " greenwashing ."

The Australian government says it has already devoted substantial sums to addressing the contamination.

According to the filing, more than 214 million Australian dollars ($153 million) has gone toward investigations, monitoring, remediation, and mitigation, and over 51 million Australian dollars ($36 million) toward research and evidence gathering.

The documents also mention legal settlements worth hundreds of millions of dollars for loss and damage, according to The Guardian.

Defense began phasing out PFAS chemicals in 2004 and stopped buying 3M's AFFF in 2003.

Even so, the filing says the chemicals have continued to leach from concrete, asphalt, soil, and sediment into groundwater and surface water, suggesting cleanup will continue.

A company spokesperson said that 3M never manufactured PFAS in Australia and had stopped selling the products at issue, while defense continued to use them.

During a hearing in Melbourne, Federal Court Justice Catherine Button commented on the scale of the dispute, saying she had "never seen a claim like this," The Guardian reported.

She added that describing the case as daunting "would be an understatement."

articles.title: FICO credit scores are holding up, but consumers are under pressure
articles.summary: Experts say that despite minimal changes to the average FICO score, affordability remains a key issue for many Americans.
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

Americans' average FICO credit score is holding steady, but experts say this number masks some affordability pressures and reveals how rising costs are shaping their financial decisions.

Today, the average U.S. FICO score sits at 714, down one point from a year ago but unchanged from October 2025, according to a new FICO® Score Credit Insights report.

A FICO credit score is a three-digit number that reflects the information in your credit reports and considers your payment history, amounts owed, credit history length, new credit, and credit mix. This score is used by lenders to make decisions about whether you qualify for mortgages, credit cards, loans, and more.

The report serves as a snapshot of consumers' credit health as rising costs tied to auto loans, housing, and credit cards put pressure on household budgets.

Affordability remains a struggle for many Americans, particularly among lower-scoring and thin-file borrowers.

The report showed that the average monthly payment for a first-time home buyer increased 57% since 2019, and mortgage balances for borrowers with scores below 620 have grown 43% since April 2019.

Auto loan balances for the lowest-scoring borrowers were also up 36%, and subsequent 90-plus-day delinquency rates for both mortgages and autos rose exclusively in the lowest-score bands, remaining flat across all higher score ranges.

"The stability we're seeing in the national average FICO score isn't necessarily because things have gotten easier for consumers — costs have risen across nearly every credit product people use, from mortgages to auto loans to credit cards," said Tommy Lee, senior director at FICO. "What's kept the average steady is that delinquency has actually improved or held steady across every major loan type. That's a story about financial discipline under pressure, not economic ease."

Delinquency remained stable or improved across most products, according to the FICO report. The share of mortgage borrowers in early-stage delinquency eased from 1.42% to 1.35% year over year, while 30-day auto delinquency improved by 5 basis points to 2.6%.

This comes on the heels of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's quarterly report on household debt and credit , which showed that credit card balances rose by $21 billion to stand at $1.26 trillion — a 1.7% increase from the previous quarter and nearing last year's high of $1.28 trillion.

Some of the strategies Americans are using to cover costs include using buy now, pay later services to keep large expenses from straining their budgets and relying on others for ongoing financial support.

Even so, it seems many Americans are still prioritizing their financial health, with nearly three-quarters of Americans checking their FICO scores multiple times a year.

"Younger consumers in particular are treating credit as a tool they're actively managing, not something that happens to them," Lee said. "That said, things have not been easy for younger generations."

He said that about 74% of Gen Z consumers rely on some form of financial support, most often from parents, and, more broadly, 37% of all Americans say the same, with 19% citing parents specifically.

"And 68% of Gen Z homeowners told us housing costs have made it harder to keep up with other expenses," Lee said. "The credit gains are real, but they're happening alongside — not in spite of — meaningful financial strain."

Tips to build and maintain a healthy FICO score

According to FICO, most creditors will consider your scores "good" if they fall between 670 and 739 (on a scale of 300 to 850), with higher scores signaling a lower-risk applicant and lower scores signaling a higher-risk applicant.

Some of the best ways to maintain a healthy score include:

Making payments on time: Payment history is the most heavily weighted factor in your score calculation, so it's important to make payments on time and avoid late or missed payments, defaults, charge-offs, collections, bankruptcies, and foreclosures.

Making more than the minimum payment to reduce your credit utilization : The second most important factor in your FICO score is the amounts owed or how much credit you're using. Working to reduce your balances by making extra payments or paying more than the minimum amount can boost your score.

Limiting new credit applications : Each time you apply for a new credit card or loan, it will result in a hard inquiry. Too many hard inquiries in a short amount of time can negatively impact your score, so it's best to avoid new applications unless absolutely necessary.

This map highlights the average credit score in every state

Here's the average credit score in each state, according to the most recent data from Experian.

Average credit score by age: How do your scores compare?

How do your credit scores compare to your peers? Here’s a breakdown of average credit scores by age, and what factors influence your credit scores.

What is a FICO score, and why should you know yours?

Learn how FICO credit scores are calculated, the different types that exist, and how to improve your FICO score fast.

Is it possible to achieve a perfect credit score of 850?

What is a perfect credit score? When using the FICO scoring model, a perfect credit score is 850. Here’s how likely it is to achieve a perfect score.

VantageScore vs. FICO: How these two major credit scoring models compare

Keeping tabs on your credit score is important. Here’s a look at the two major credit scoring models — VantageScore and FICO — and how they differ.

Decent credit can mean more opportunities and lower rates on loans and insurance. If you're wondering what a good credit score is, here's what to know.

"Younger consumers in particular are treating credit as a tool they're actively managing, not something that happens to them," Lee said. "That said, things have not been easy for younger generations."
He said that about 74% of Gen Z consumers rely on some form of financial support, most often from parents, and, more broadly, 37% of all Americans say the same, with 19% citing parents specifically.

"And 68% of Gen Z homeowners told us housing costs have made it harder to keep up with other expenses," Lee said. "The credit gains are real, but they're happening alongside — not in spite of — meaningful financial strain."
Tips to build and maintain a healthy FICO score

According to FICO, most creditors will consider your scores "good" if they fall between 670 and 739 (on a scale of 300 to 850), with higher scores signaling a lower-risk applicant and lower scores signaling a higher-risk applicant.
Some of the best ways to maintain a healthy score include:

Making payments on time: Payment history is the most heavily weighted factor in your score calculation, so it's important to make payments on time and avoid late or missed payments, defaults, charge-offs, collections, bankruptcies, and foreclosures.

Making more than the minimum payment to reduce your credit utilization : The second most important factor in your FICO score is the amounts owed or how much credit you're using. Working to reduce your balances by making extra payments or paying more than the minimum amount can boost your score.

Limiting new credit applications : Each time you apply for a new credit card or loan, it will result in a hard inquiry. Too many hard inquiries in a short amount of time can negatively impact your score, so it's best to avoid new applications unless absolutely necessary.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy's Last Words to Her 3 Kids Before Their Deaths Revealed
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy’s last words to her and husband Patrick Clancy's three kids before their 2023 deaths were revealed as Dr. Kirk Heilbrun testified in the trial...
articles.body:
Content warning: This story discusses violence against children and suicidal ideation.

New details are coming to light in the Lindsay Clancy case.

During court proceedings for the 36-year-old—who is on trial for three counts of first-degree murder after admitting to killing her and then-husband Patrick Clancy 's kids Cora , 5, Dawson , 3 and Callan , 8 months, in 2023—forensic psychologist Dr. Kirk Heilbrun revealed the last words that the former labor and delivery nurse told her children before strangling them and trying to kill herself.

During his testimony Aug. 24, which was livestreamed by Associated Press , Heilbrun—who evaluated Lindsay for three days in April—testified that she killed her children as part of what he described as "altruistic filicide," saying she believed they would suffer without her and that killing them would allow them to be "together in heaven."

As she killed them, she told the children, according to Heilbrun, "Go to God, baby. Go to God."

The psychologist also revealed what Lindsay said to Patrick after he returned home and asked what she had done. According to Heilbrun, she replied, "I tried to kill myself."

Dolly Parton, Country Music Legend, Dead at 80

Dolly Parton Shared How She Wanted to Be Remembered Before Death

Lindsay admitted to strangling her three children to death using an exercise band in January 2023 before attempting to take her own life by jumping out of a second-story window. She suffered a fall that left her paralyzed from the waist down.

While she has not denied killing her three kids, Lindsay has pleaded not guilty for criminal responsibility in their murders due to her state of mind during the incident, which her defense attorney Kevin Reddington is arguing was compromised due to postpartum psychosis.

Heilbrun said Lindsay's response to Patrick was inconsistent with psychosis, noting that someone experiencing hallucinations likely would have replied differently.

However, he also noted that Lindsay shared with him that she did hear a male voice about 18 minutes before the murders, which said, "Kill the kids so you can kill yourself."

"The way she described this as happening is that she heard a voice that she'd never heard before, experienced a hallucination and she's never experienced it since. But she only experienced it for the 18 minutes or so that it took to kill the children," Heilbrun testified. "To put it mildly, that would be a very, very unusual pattern or manifestation of how this kind of thing comes about. Very unusual."

Heilbrun told the court he diagnosed Lindsay with Bipolar II disorder. Saying she experienced both manic and depressive episodes, he admitted the diagnosis was difficult to reach "because of all the diagnoses in the records and all the symptoms that she experienced."

Heilbrun also brought up Lindsay's Catholic faith, which prompted Reddington to request a mistrial. Judge William Sullivan denied the motion.

images.caption: Jonathan Wiggs/The Boston Globe via Getty Images

Lindsay Clancy 's now-ex-husband was the first witness called to testify during her murder trial, which began July 27 in Plymouth Superior Court. The 35-year-old former nurse has not denied killing daughter Cora , 5, and sons Dawson , 3, and Callan , 8 months, but has pleaded not guilty of murder, the defense attributing her actions to postpartum psychosis. Patrick Clancy testified that Lindsay struggled with her mental health after giving birth to Callan in May 2023, according to CNN . She also sought treatment after Dawson was born in 2019, he said, "but it didn't last very long." Lindsay's "big spiral," as he referred to it, occurred in December 2023 after she started taking a new medication, one of several she'd been prescribed since September, Patrick said. He testified that Lindsay told him she had "intrusive thoughts" about harming their children and herself. He didn't worry about the kids' safety, he said, because she didn't seem to have "any intention" of actually hurting them. On Dec. 31, Patrick said, Lindsay went to the E.R. at Massachusetts General Hospital "because she was still talking about thoughts of suicide . She was admitted to an affiliated psychiatric facility, and when she was discharged Jan. 5 she seemed "much better."

On Jan. 24, 2023, Lindsay "was having one of her best days," Patrick testified, per CNN , recalling that his then-wife built a snowman in the yard. "She was playing with the kids," he said, "and she seemed in a good mood." That morning she had taken Cora to a doctor's appointment and he had texted her a picture of Dawson after he "dressed himself completely for the first time." Patrick told the court he had felt "hopeful" since his wife's release from the hospital. "Her mood seemed better," he said. "She was more active, and she was able...to partake in more things." Before he left to pick up dinner and medication for Cora, he said he kissed one of the kids on the head and told them he'd "be right back." Prosecutors allege Lindsay sent Patrick on errands to get him out of the house on purpose. Then, Plymouth County Assistant District Attorney Shanan Buckingham said in her opening statement, she strangled the children with exercise bands "deliberately and meticulously." Patrick testified July 29 that no one told him he shouldn't leave Linday alone with their kids, telling the court, "I didn't know what psychosis was until after this happened."

In the audio recording of Patrick's seven-minute 911 call that was played in court July 29, according to the Associated Press , he's heard telling the dispatcher, who repeatedly asks what happened, "She killed the kids!"

Lindsay wrote about her struggles, including that she felt "incredibly sad and guilty" about not breastfeeding Callan, according to journal excerpts read to jurors Aug. 5. "I want help," she wrote in an entry read by her attorney. "I want to be well." In another, she said, "I have crazy brain fog. I feel like I can't make a plan. I live moment to moment waiting for the next nap time. I'm terrified of Cal getting overtired now because I feel can't help him."

When Lindsay was hospitalized after killing her children and allegedly tried to take her own life, she tested positive for the antidepressant mirtazapine, the mood stabilizer lamotrigine, the antidepressant trazodone and quetiapine, a drug used to treat schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and severe depression, forensic toxicologist Justin Brower testified Aug. 5. He said, per The Guardian , that his lab found that only the level of quetiapine in her blood was slightly elevated, but it wasn't at a "toxic" or "suicidal concentration." He further described the levels in her blood as "not consistent" with someone who takes a bunch of pills before trying to end her life. Under defense cross-examination, Brower also said that toxicology results "don't tell the entire story." Lindsay's attorney Kevin Reddington said in his July 28 opening statement that she has bipolar disorder and medication worsened her condition. On the day she killed Cora, Dawson and Callan, Reddington said, she heard a voice telling her, "'This is your last chance. Kill the children so you can kill yourself.'"

The Clancy family's nanny Elaine Rossi testified Aug. 5 that she had no concerns about Lindsay's fitness as a mother. "I observed a wonderful mom who loved her kids," Rossi said. "She was concerned about their safety, and Callan eating and sleeping. She was a wonderful mother."

Andrea Hennigan , who previously worked with the defendant at Massachusetts General, testified Aug. 6 that Lindsay told her at lunch after Callan was born that she didn't plan to go back to work as a labor-and-delivery nurse because she "was not in a mental state to take care of patients." "She talked about insomnia and not feeling herself," Hennigan said, per the AP . "I believe she might have used the words brain fog or something like that." Lindsay texted her in January 2023, Hennigan said, that she was experiencing "bad or negative side effects" from medication.

articles.title: Winter energy prices expected to rise to three year high
articles.summary: Millions of households will be affected by an increase in the energy price cap by regulator Ofgem.
articles.body:
Energy bills for millions of households are expected to rise this winter to the highest level for three years, under a price cap to be announced by the industry regulator on Wednesday.

The cap will reflect the rise in the wholesale cost of gas, paid by suppliers and will hit bills just as the colder weather arrives in October until the end of December.

Analysts expect Ofgem to say prices will go up by 4% compared with the current cap, affecting those on variable tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales.

Firms say energy debt has jumped and, with high bills likely to persist, have called for more support for those struggling to pay. The government says VAT is being cut from electricity bills.

The price cap for about 33 million households is expected to rise, driven by volatility in international wholesale gas prices.

The average price of gas has been 61% higher over the past three months compared to late 2025, according to suppliers' trade body Energy UK.

Millions of people have moved on to fixed energy tariffs, some in response to the uncertainty created by the impact of the US-Israeli war with Iran.

Anyone on a fixed deal will not see the price they pay rise, until at least the end of the term of their tariff. About 40% of billpayers have fixed tariffs.

The energy cap sets a maximum price for each unit of gas and electricity, not the total bill, so a household's final bill depends on what they use.

In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back owing to high prices of recent years while energy efficiency has improved.

Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year.

Cornwall Insight, the consultancy, has forecast that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity, paid through direct debit, will pay £1,729 a year from October.

This is up from £1,663 between July and September and woild be the highest for three years.

You could be missing out on £150 off your energy bill - here's how to check

What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills?

Households are paying hundreds of pounds a year more on average than before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 started the energy crisis. Bills have gone up by about 70% compared with the pre-crisis norm, according to industry data.

That means unpaid bills and charges have shot up. Energy UK estimates total debt to have collectively risen to £6bn, with an expectation of it to increase to about £7bn by the end of the year.

The average billpayer in debt, without a payment plan, owed £3,500, it said.

The trade body has called for a flexible discounted tariff for those most in need, funded by taxation. That is supported by many debt charities.

"Without urgent intervention – namely a national social tariff and implementation of the long-awaited debt write off scheme from Ofgem – we expect this [debt] figure to rise in the coming months, and with that see an increase in the number of people coming to us for help with energy bills," said Emily Whitford, senior public policy advocate at StepChange.

The Trades Union Congress has called for a windfall tax on bank profits to be used to reduce energy bills.

The government is cutting VAT from electricity bills in October , which should knock about £50 off a typical annual bill, and some policy costs were cancelled or shifted in April, but ministers say there is more to do.

Suppliers offer a host of support schemes to anyone struggling to pay, or who is likely to find it difficult.

Energy UK has a list of these schemes . But it stresses that companies can often only help if you get in touch with your supplier to tell them you are unable to pay.

Three reasons why UK electricity prices are so high
